Sir THOMAS WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved the second leading of Bill No. 53, respecting insurance.
He said:	This legislation is rendered
necessary by a decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in what is known as The Insurance Case, which was decided in March of last year. The Bill repeals the Insurance Act of 1910 and Te-enaots it with certain amendments. The amendments are of two classes:	First,
those which are necessary to remove from the existing Act the features which have

been ruled by the decision of the Privy Council in The Insurance Case to be ultra vire6, and, second, those considered necessary to meet changed conditions which have arisen since the passing of the present Act and to remove serious defects which have come to light in the course of its administration. The decision of the Privy Council to which I have alluded is the culmination of considerable litigation which has from time to time during the last twenty years concerned itself with the question of the constitutionality of the Insurance Act. The point as to the constitutionality of the Insurance Act, however, never came up squarely in the course of the litigation to which I have referred. It arose incidentally from time to time, and as a result of the doulbt which was cast upon the constitutionality of the Act, a reference was made by the Solicitor General of Canada to the Supreme Court to determine the question. The Supreme Court gave its decision, and the case was afterwards appealed to the Privy Council. In 1909 it was held by Judge Lett, sitting as magistrate in ihe city of Montreal, that the Insurance Act was ultra vires and that it was not po&sible to enforce the penalties provided by the Act for infractions of the law. As a result, the administration of the Insurance Act was practically paralyzed.

On what
ground?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On the ground that it was ultra vires of the Dominion Parliament.
What particular part of the Act was declared ultra vires, and to what part of the case did it refer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The case was the King vs. Willis Faber & Company, who, unlicensed, had been soliciting insurance and collecting premiums in violation of a provision of the Act as in force at that time, which is now section 4 of the Insurance Act.
The magistrate held that the license could be issued only by the provincial government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was held that the legislature of the Dominion, in requiring a company or person to obtain a license before carrying on the business of insurance in Canada, was ultra vires of the Dominion.
That matter belonged to the provinces only?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not sure as to what further was decided, but that was the point so far as Dominion legislation was concerned. There was no appeal from that decision, and the result was that the administration of the Insurance Act has been practically paralyzed ever since becanse of the impossibility of enforcing the penalties provided for infractions of the law. The matter came squarely before the Privy Council as to the constitutionality of sections 4 and 70 of the Act. Section 4 of the Act is as follows:
In Canada, except as otherwise provided by this Act, no company or underwriters or 'other person shall solicit or accept any risk, or issue or deliver any receipt or policy of insurance, or grant any annuity on a life or lives, or collect or receive any premium, or inspect any risk, or adjust any loss, or carry on any business of insurance, or prosecute or maintain any suit, action or proceeding, or file any claim in insolvency relating to such business, unless it be done by or on behalf of a company or underwriters holding a license from the minister.
In other words, the Act prohibits any company or person from carrying on the business of insurance in Canada without obtaining a license from the Dominion Government. I should explain that that section applied not only to companies incorporated by the Dominion Parliament and to persons throughout the Dominion, but to companies incorporated by the provinces carrying on business outside such provinces. The Privy Council decided that section 4 was ultra vires of the Dominion Parliament. The terms of its decision in that connection are as follows:
Their Lordships are therefore of opinion that the majority in the Supreme Court were right in answering the first of the two questions referred to them in the affirmative.
That is to say, the effect of the decision of the Supreme Court, afterwards confirmed by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, was that sections 4 and 70-the latter being the section providing penalties for infractions of the Act-were ultra vires of the Parliament of Canada. Although the question asks whether the sections are ultra vires of the Parliament of Canada, and specifically inquires as to whether "any and what part or parts of the said sections" are ultra vires of the Parliament of Canada, the Privy Council has contented itself with stating that sections 4 and 70 are ultra vires. The result is that the validity of sections 4 and 70-and, by consequence, of the whole Insurance Act, because section 4 is a basic and fundamental section of the
Act-is impugned by the decision of the Privy Council.	.
The Privy Council has not stated whether any particular provision or provisions of section 4 of the Insurance Act are intra vires; it simply states that section 4 is ultra vires, but it is to be gathered from the context of the judgment of the Privy Council that the Judicial Committee is of the opinion that it is beyond the powers of Parliament to require a provincially incorporated insurance company to obtain a license from the minister, even if the company extends its business to provinces other than that by which it was incorporated. I may say that the existing Act, that is to say, the Insurance Act of 1910, withdraws from its application the provincially incorporated company which restricts its business to its own province, but requires it to obtain a Dominion license in the event of its extending its business beyond that province; that is to say, under the Dominion Act of 1910, a provincially incorporated company doing business solely within its own province was not required to obtain a license, but if it extended its business beyond the confines of its province, then by section 4 of the Insurance Act it was required to obtain a license from the Dominion Government. The most important change in the new Bill, therefore, arising out of the constitutional question-and I am discussing the constitutional question and the amendments necessary to meet the decision first-is the withdrawal from the application of the Act of all provincially incorporated companies save those which voluntarily obtain a license from the minister. Just let me repeat that. The new Bill, now before the House, excludes from its operation provincially incorporated companies whether they carry on their business solely within the province or beyond its jurisdiction. It seems to be necessary that they all should be excluded in order to come within the requirements of the judgment of the Privy Council. In order to meet the case of provincially incorporated companies which may desire voluntarily to take out licenses under the Dominion Insurance Act, provision is made in the Bill whereby such companies, if they elect to come in, are regarded as Canadian companies for the purposes of the Act.
I think I can summarize in a sentence what I have said as to provincially incorporated companies. The effect is that unless a provincially incorporated company voluntarily seeks a license under the Act, it is completely exempt from the provisions of the Act; but if it seeks and obtains such



a license, it becomes a Canadian company, and so becomes subject to the Act to the same extent as those Canadian companies originally incorporated by Parliament.
There is another question of an important character involved in the decision of the Privy Council and dealt with in this House, and that is as to whether the Dominion Parliament has jurisdiction to require a foreign insurance	company-and	by
" foreign " I include British-to take out a license even in a case where a company desires to carry on its business only within the limits of a single province. The answer which the Privy Council gave upon that side of the case was that it was " within the power of Parliament, by properly framed legislation "-I am reading from their lordships' decision-to impose such a restriction as it appears that such power is given by section 91 of the British North America Act, which refers to the regulation of trade and commerce and to aliens. In other words, their lordships say that by properly framed legislation the Dominion Parliament may enact legislation of an authoritative and binding character upon foreign insurance companies, and they found that jurisdiction upon section 91 of the British North America Act, which, of course, in the division of subjects between the provinces and the Dominion, allocates to the Dominion the subjects of trade and commerce and aliens. The suggestion, however, of their lordships that the Dominion might do this by properly framed legislation is an intimation that the existing legislation is inadequate, and therefore the sections of the Bill now before the House which require British and foreign companies to obtain a license under it are so worded as to show that the power assumed is taken under the heads which I have mentioned, namely, trade and commerce and aliens. This Bill, before being brought before the House, has received the most careful consideration on the part not only of the Insurance Department, but of the Deputy Minister of Justice and of outside counsel, in order to bring its provisions within the judgment of the Judicial Committee in the insurance case, and strictly within the powers of enactment of the Dominion Parliament. That is all I, have to say upon the constitutional aspect of the matter. All the constitutional changes are to be found in sections two to twelve, inclusive, of . this Bill.

The question as to the right of locally incorporated companies to do business in other provinces than that in which they are incorporated has been hack
TSir Thomas White.]
and forth before the courts for a number of years, and it has also been before the Privy Council. I am not familiar as to how that question stands now, and that question is involved in the question that the minister is now discussing. Suppose an insurance company, incorporated by the province of Ontario, starts to do business in the province of Quebec, would this Government have a right to give that Ontario incorporated company a license to do business in the province of Quebec? I understand the minister has taken power by this legislation to give that Ontario company such a license. I would be afraid that we would have no jurisdiction to enable a local company that has power to do business only in Ontario to go into Quebec or any other province to do business there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: What limit do you make?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The amendment provides that such companies which have an unimpaired capital may on complying with such conditions as may be required by the Treasury Board, including the maintenance of deposits in excess of that ordinarily required, obtain licenses under the Act. The maximum amount of excess deposit which may be required is left at $200,000, as in the existing Act, but the minimum excess deposit of $50,000 for a license for fire or life insurance, and of $10,000 for a license for other classes has been removed. I may say that this has been done upon the recommendation of the Superintendent of Insurance who has gone into the matter carefully. It seems to me to be on the whole a wise amendment.
Then provision is made to permit of contracts of fire insurance and automobile insurance being combined in a single policy.
There is a further provision prohibiting any company from issuing a financial state-
133$
ment including in the surplus of the company the amount of the subscribed or paid up capital, unless the amount of such subscribed or paid up capital is specifically stated and mentioned as included in the surplus. It also requires that a statement containing figures showing the amount of the subscribed capital shall also show the amount paid thereon, and if the statement shows the authorized capital, it shall also show the subscribed and paid up capital. The amendment is designed to abolish the practice, somewhat common, of issuing financial statements showing huge surpluses to policyholders, which surpluses are made up almost wholly of subscribed but unpaid capital. For instance, a company may have a subscribed capital of $2,000,000, but a more or less worthless set of shareholders. Now if that company shows in its statements to the public its subscribed capital, we are making it show its paid up capital, also the idea being, of course, to protect the public.
Then there are some important amendments arising out of conditions disclosed at the time the Union Life Insurance Company became insolvent and was wound up. The House may remember that the Superintendent of Insurance became liquidator, and as the result of reinsurance effected with the Metropolitan Life a great catastrophe was averted. There were some 150,000 or 160,000 policyholders in that company. It carried on "industrial" insurance. We found that the present Act does not lend itself to insistence by the Superintendent of Insurance upon reinsurance. It is very difficult when a company becomes insolvent to force the directors to take the action which is necessary to protect the policyholders. The action that is indicated in most cases of that kind is clearly reinsurance, but there was no provision in the Act of 1910 empowering the Superintendent of Insurance or the minister to say to the directors of the company in a clear case, after every opportunity has been given to put the company in a solvent condition, "Now you must reinsure." We are now taking power to do that. It was found in connection with the Union Life that it was possible under the existing Act to make improvident contracts extending say over a course of twenty years. If the company was thrown into insolvency the holder of that contract would rank for the value of his contract with other creditors upon the proceeds. It was felt by the Insurance Department and by the Government that there should be legislation to prevent the entering into of contracts of that kind, and there

is provision in the present legislation to meet that situation. It relates, of course, to contracts burdensome to companies.
Then we have a section which deals with the powers of investment of insurance companies. In section 58 it is provided, in subsection 2, that any provincial company which obtains a license under this Act and which has unauthorized securities among its investments, shall dispose of the same within five years from the date of the issue of the Dominion license. Under the present Act provincial companies obtaining a Dominion license probably retain the powers of investment granted by their provincial charters. It is now proposed that such companies obtaining a Dominion license shall have their investment powers curtailed or enlarged to conform with the provisions of the Act.
That is to say, if a provincially incorporated company, by its own voluntary action, submits itself to the jurisdiction of the Dominion, then its power of investment must be curtailed to conform to the investment requirements of the Dominion Insurance Act. There are other provisions which limit the power of a Canadian company to invest in the stock of any other company which is transacting, or authorized to transact, the same class of insurance. That is to prevent interlocking, so to speak, of directorates and businesses. Then we have the further protection to policy-holders, and to the public, in that we have provided that the directors of the company shall be responsible for the replacing of certain unauthorized investments. It has been specially drawn to the attention of the department and to the minister that directors will, notwithstanding the plain terms of the Insurance Act, make unauthorized investments, and the Superintendent of Insurance does not become aware of it until the damage is done. Under the present Act, there appears to be no effectual provision for dealing with directors who make such unauthorized investments, and we have attempted to remedy that in the present Bill.
There is another important amendment, relating to hail insurance companies. Some of these companies have been carrying on business without proper safeguards, so far as the public is concerned. I do not make a sweeping statement, but I say that some of them at all events carry on business without providing an adequate reserve fund. In this Bill there is provision that Canadian companies shall accumulate their profits until a reserve fund is established equal to

at least 50 per cent of the premiums received during the preceding calendar year. That is a necessary safeguard in the interests of the public, and especially of the farming community who take out hail insurance.
There are further provisions in the new Act, giving the Insurance Department and the Treasury Board greater share of control over insurance companies in the organization stage. Without going into details, I may say that these safeguards are similar to those thrown around the organization of banks, under the Bank Act. Hon. members may recall that that subject was dis-cused pretty fully before the Banking and Commerce Committee on the last revision of the Bank Act, and subsequently in the House.
This is an important measure, involving the re-acting .of the present Insurance Act, with the amendments which I have indicated. I should not have brought it down this session, the House being engaged principally in business arising out of the war, save for the fact that the administration of the Act is paralyzed on account of the doubt cast on the entire legislation by the decision of the Pirivy 'Council. I may say, further, that it is not possible to accomplish what we have in mind by a mere amending of the Act, because it has been necessary to define terms and use phraseology not used in the existing act, and as a result we have been obliged to bring down a Bill covering the entire field.

I understand the minister's declaration to mean that a company incorporated by a provincial legislature is fully authorized to carry on business within the province, without any control from the Dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Without a license, report, inspection, or anything at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the position.

I am very sorry to hear
that, because- it is contrary to the public sentiment in Quebec and is a very bad provision. I think, if all insurance companies *were made responsible to the Dominion it would be in the public interest.

Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No.

54, to amend the Criminal Code Respecting Insurance.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This Bill is in reality the complement of the Bill which has just been read the second time on the motion of the Minister of Finance. Substantially, this Bill makes it an offence under the Criminal Code for any person to engage in the business of insurance, unless he has obtained, or is acting on behalf -of a company which has obtained, the license provided for in the Bill which has been read the second time. There is just one enacting provision; the others are details. The reason this matter is dealt with by an amendment to the Criminal Code is, perhaps, to be found in the observation which the hon. gentleman from Bonaventure just made in connection with the other Bill, namely, that it is a matter of general public interest that there should be effective supervision and control over the business of insurance throughout the Dominion of Canada, and so important was it that there should be that control effectively exercised, and so much was the public exposed to serious deception, entailing serious loss and damage, if there were not that control, that it would 'be a perfectly proper thing to look upon it as a public wrong-in other words, a crime-for a company to carry on that business without subjecting itself to the supervision and control provided under the Insurance Act. It may be said that that might very well be provided in the Insurance Act. I am not prepared to dispute the soundness of that proposition, but it was thought well, in view of some things that were said in the course of the litigation to which the Minister of Finance has referred, to make it quite clear that Parliament, in taking upon itself to make it an offence to carry on the business of insurance otherwise than in conformity with the provisions of the Insurance Act, was dealing with the matter as a public wrong, and that, in enacting legislation providing for punishment Parliament should avowedly and expressly, proceed under its power to deal with the criminal law. I do not desire to suggest that the same argument might not have been made, and perhaps just as effectively, if these provisions had been embodied' in the Act itself. But it was thought wiser, in view of past experience and the result of previous legislation, to take every precaution that could be taken to meet the suggestion that the legislation might perhaps be open to question as coming under any other powers of this Parliament, by making it quite clear that Parliament, at all events as far as its views of the matter and the manner in which it approached it might bear upon it, looked upon the matter and dealt with it as a proper subject for criminal legislation and in the exercise of its exclusive power to deal with the criminal law.
What was the charge against the individuals who were brought before Judge Leet and in regard to which he said that this Parliament had exceeded its authority?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: and finally toy the Privy Council upon a reference 'by this Government to 4 p.m. the Supreme Court in the first instance of the question of the constitutionality of this particular section, and the fact that this judgment had been rendered by the magistrate was, I think, one of the many other circumstances which led the then Government to consider that it was a proper thing to have the question submitted and decided.
What was the final judgment rendered by the Privy Council? There was so much noise that I could not hear the Finance Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As the Minister of Finance pointed out, the Privy Council held, affirming the judgment of the Supreme Court, that section 4 of the Act of 1910 was ultra vires of the Parliament of Canada, that the Par'iament of Canada had no constitutional power to enact section 4 which prohibited the carrying on of the insurance business generally save by companies obtaining licenses from the Government of Canada or by persons acting on behalf of such companies. The Privy Council held that in that general enactment the Parliament of Canada had exceeded its powers. I have not before me the text of the judgment, or the reasoning that leads up to this finding, and which is endeavoured to be met in the provisions of the Bill which has just passed its second reading.

I repeat that there was so much noise, and the accous-tics of this House are so bad, that I could not hear. But, I understood my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance, to say that their lordships of the Privy Council had expressed the opinion that this Parliament would have the power to pass properly framed legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was dealing
with the question of foreign insurance companies carrying on business in Canada. Their lordships expressed the opinion that the Dominion Parliament, under its jurisdiction as to trade and. commerce and aliens, could pass legislation requiring such companies to take out a license before they could carry on business in Canada, and their lordships expressed the view that the Dominion Parliament could do that on properly framed legislation. That seemed to imply that the legislation at present existing, that is to say, the Insurance Act of 1910, was not properly framed. In this Bill they have endeavoured to so frame the

legislation as to bring it within the terms of their lordships' judgment. In the section dealing with foreign insurance companies Parliament assumes jurisdiction by special reference to its powers under section 91 of the British North America Act relating to trade and commerce and aliens. With regard to provincially incorporated companies, their lordships' judgment appears to be clear that the Dominion Parliament has no authority over these.

What I have to say might properly have been said when, my hon friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) had his Insurance Bill before the House. We seem, by this judgment of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, to have got the insurance business into somewhat of a muddle. I am srory, that is the position. It strikes me that the better way, on behalf of the public, is to have the insurance business controlled by one head and that head the Insurance Department of the Dominion. Under this decision we seem to have five different standards. We have the provincial company operating in the province in which it has got its charter; we have the company with a provincial charter operating outside of its own province; we have the foreign one operating in one or two provinces; then we have the federal one operating anywhere in Canada. The difficulty is a bit serious. The company with a federal charter is subject to all the restrictions of all the Insurance Acts passed by this Parliament and it must be admitted that these restrictions, while necessary, are quite severe in some instances. That is, while they protect the public, they hamper some businesses that might be considered legitimate by the ordinary business concern but are not so considered on account of the ramifications of the business of an insurance company. Now we have the provincial company operating in competition with the federal company without these restrictions. It strikes me that it would be almost necessary, if it were possible, for the provinces and the federal authority to get together and arrive at some basis of restriction which would be incorporated in all the Acts because if that be not done, two companies side by side and doing business with the same people may be operating under different Acts altogether, which would not be for the public good and certainly would not be for the good of the companies. The provinces, of course, under section 92 of the British North America Act, have the

right to impose licenses where a company is operating within their borders, whether it be a federal company or a provincial company. Each province, generally speaking, has given to municipalities in it the right to impose further taxation, so that the federal company finds itself now in the position of having to take out a license with the Dominion, another with each province, and another with each municipality, making the . company that has a federal charter a much more expensive institution to conduct than the one that takes out a provincial charter.
There is another question that strikes me as important, and perhaps the minister has provided for it in his Bill. Under the present Act, no company gets credit in its report for re-insurance in another company that has not a federal license. Now the question will arise immediately, will this Bill provide that re-insurance in a provincial company, though it has not a federal charter, will be credited to the company taking out that re-insurance when it comes to make its report to the Finance Department. It is a serious matter, particularly to younger companies. I suggest to the minister that this is something worth thinking about in arranging the details of this Act, because he can readily see that many provincial companies may have charters, and I am inclined to think that they will in many instances confine themselves to the provincial charters, as the provincial restrictions are not now as severe as those 'imposed on federally-incorporated companies. Before the Bill goes into committee, I would suggest to the minister that he think that matter over, as it is one of vital importance.
There is one more point, which the minister and I have discussed privately, that is the valuation of securities held by these companies. Under the present system of the department, which has prevailed for very many years, when the valuation of securities comes to be made at the end of the year, the market values at the time the report is made are taken as the basis of valuation. Under present conditions, with the war on, some securities fluctuate very materially. Take a municipal security purchased some years ago when the rate of interest was low. Now that security is gilt edged, there never will be any default; when it matures it will be paid, one hundred cents on the dollar. Under the present system only the price that the security would bring in the market at the present time is allowed by the department. One can
readily see that with the present demand for money, the Dominion Finance Minister himself being a competitor in the money market, the price of money has very materially increased, and the municipal or other security of the company paying a small rate of interest is naturally low-priced; while its intrinsic value remains the same, it has perhaps depreciated ten points or fifteen points in market value, and the company holding that security has deducted from its assets the loss in market value of this security. I rather criticised that method of making the valuation before the war, hut surely it is worthy of consideration at the present time. We might consider whether, under all the circumstances, that rule could not be deviated from as liberally as possible, because the minister can see, perhaps better than any person else, that a young company will show a loss perhaps from the fact that its investments are gilt edged municipal securities, whereas if it had invested in other securities not of the same intrinsic value it might show a gain because of the present fluctuations in the value of such securities. I suggest to the minister that in the framing of his Act he should endeavour to find some means of meeting that difficulty, because the situation may become quite serious if carried to an extreme. At my request, the minister has had a line added at the bottom of the annual report pointing out the reinsurance in foreign countries, so that notice is taken of it; but it is not included in the totals, and people lose sight of that-particularly. a competing agent always forgets to read that line to his prospects.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.
. Mr. DOHERTY: I move that this Bill be referred to the Banking and Commerce Committee. As I pointed out, it really is a complement of the Insurance Bill proper, and I think it can be most conveniently dealt with at the same time and by the same committee.
Motion agreed to.

Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and lisheries) moved the second reading of Bill No. 69, to repeal the Ocean Telegraph Act. He said: I explained this proposed legislation when the resolution upon which it is based was under consideration. Under the Ocean Telegraph Act, which was passed m 1913, an agreement between the Governor of Canada and the Universal Radio Syndicate, Limited, was confirmed. Under this agreement the syndicate was to establish one radio station in Canada and one in Great Britain for the transmission of messages at rates not to exceed certain stated amounts, and the Government agreed to issue the necessary license for that pur-
returned to the syndicate when it had expended $50,000, $25,000 of which was to foe expended in Canada. The balance was to foe repaid to the syndicate upon the completion of proper equipment and the satisfactory operation of the stations in the United Kingdom and in Canada, the Government to allow interest on the deposit at the rate which the banks allowed the Government upon its deposits. The syndicate also had the right, under the agreement, to be thereafter incorporated. They made the required expenditure, and $25,000 of the deposit was returned. Owing to the outbreak of war the syndicate was unable to float a company to operate the stations and to acquire the necessary apparatus. The syndicate being in urgent need of money, the Governor in Council, having regard to the value of a second transatlantic radiotelegraph service, and after consultation with the British Post Office authorities, loaned the syndicate, at their request, the sum of $15,000, to bear interest at the rate of 5 per cent and to be repaid on May 1, 1915. An official test of the service which was conducted on January 27, 1915, established that the operating speed and general performance of the station was not up to the standard called for by the agreement. Payment of the balance of the deposit was accordingly withheld. The syndicate is now quite unable to carry out the terms of its agreement, and the Governor in Council has refused to exercise the power under the agreement of purchasing the station, though at present use is being made of the station in Canada, which is situated in Newcastle, N.B. It is now proposed to repeal the Act and to return to the syndicate the balance of the deposit, less the amount due for the loan made foy the Crown.
There are only two sections in the Bill, one repealing the Act and the other authorizing the return of the amount of the deposit now in the hands of the Government. The company is now in the hands of a receiver, but the Marconi Company have made arrangements with the receiver to take over the station, thoroughly equip it and make it first-class in every way. Before doing so, however, they wish us to repeal this Act, to relieve the station of any lien we may have upon it, and to return the balance of the deposit which is in our hands. To accomplish this is the purpose of the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, personally I am glad that this

friend, and 1 will support it very cheerfully. The Marconi company has an excellent reputation throughout the world, and I believe the Marconi system, firmly established in Canada as it is in Europe, will result in giving cheaper rates for the transmission of messages between America and Europe. I am not surprised that the Poulsen system has not been a success. When that legislation was introduced in 1913 by the former Postmaster General, Hon. Mr. Pelletier, I ventured to predict that he was moving too quickly in the matter, and that the Poulsen system, from what I had heard in Europe at the time I was negotiating for cheaper cable rates, was far from being up to the mark. He chose, however, to proceed with his legislation, and he promised us wonders as the result of the establishment of that system in Canada, but the net result of his efforts have been that we have had no system at all and that there has been the old cable monopoly. The Marconi system will, I believe, be a real benefit, and will tend to bring about a reduction in the rates. We need competition in this regard. The Administration of which I formed part, is responsible for the reduction in cable rates which took place between Great Britain and Canada. It was at our request that the cable companies gave first the cheap rates for the press, secondly the cheap week-end rates, and thirdly, the deferred cables, which also mean a reduction in the rates; but I said that at that time that if we could make arrangements with the Marconi company, we would create such a competition in Canada in the rates between Canada and Great Britain that before long the consumers would feel that the expense of corresponding by means of Marconigraan or cablegram was not too great.
I am glad that this matter has been transferred from the Post Office Department, which apparently has no head at the present time, to the care of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, because he is most progressive and he stands very firmly for British connection, and one of the aims I had when I advocated cheap cable rates was the promotion of closer connection between Canada and the Mother Country. We have in Western Canada especially, and also in Eastern Canada, a large proportion of British immigrants, and this country will, in the years to come, receive a large influx of immigrants from the British Isles. Although the postal rates have been increased on account of the war, they will be reduced again to
the penny standard; and whilst we have cheap postal rates, yet for the benefit of our British immigration we should have cheap Marconi and cheap cable rates also. One of the men who worked most energetically in favour of those cheap rates was the late Sir John Henniker Heaton who sat for 24 years in the British House of Commons, and who was called the Postmaster General-at-Large of the British Empire. Through his efforts and through the efforts of my predecessor, Sir William Mulock, penny post was established, and afterwards the question of cable and Marconi rates came before the Imperial conference each time it met. The House will remember that on many occasions resolutions more academic than practical were adopted by the House, and I do not know whether at the conference which the Prime Minister attended this year a similar resolution was adopted to that adopted on previous occasions. At all events this is a step in the right direction, and I hope my hon. friend in granting this privilege to the Marconi company will see to it that the work is proceeded with, that the rates are duly controlled by him, and that such measures are taken that the consumers in Canada shall benefit by those rates.
I happen to know-the gentlemen who are interested in the Canadian Marconi Company, and I may say that they are most responsible, they belong to the best elements in our business community; and I dare say that under their leadership we shall have before long a really cheap rate for correspondence by means of Marconi-gram between Canada and Europe, and that in this' way we shall establish a competition which will bring the cable companies to their senses.

Mr. Speaker, I remember when the legislation was introduced in this House by the late Postmaster General, and I heard my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) address the House on that question. I also spoke, and I took the stand then that, instead of making a deal with this private company, we should devote our efforts and our energies to the establishment of a cheap state-owned or Empire-owned cable system with a view to a better service between the mother country and America. I said further that I had no doubt at that time that this company, which had entered into an arrangement with the Government which arrangement has now fallen down, was, at bottom, in alliance with the great cable monopoly that

controls the service in every part of the world.
That is quite possible.

A report has been presented by the commission, of which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) is a member, in favour of an Imperial cable system. We have such a system now between Australia and Canada, and for years we have been asking for an Empire-owned system between Canada and the mother country, and all the time somebody is putting it off. This proposal which was introduced some years ago and which has now failed according to the statement made here to-day, has proved this, that it was for the purpose not of giving good service, but of blocking for a time a publicly-owned service.
Instead of adopting the report of the Koyal Commission we are now dealing with another privately-owned company; the problem will never be solved in that way. ^ I think the minister in introducing this legislation should acquaint the House with the report made by the Royal Commission, of which Sir George Foster was a member. The report shows that by reason of the war and the increase in trade there should be an Atlantic cable owned by the. state. That is where the paying traffic is. Whenever anybody proposes public ownership of a public utility the invariable answer is: Try it out in some outlying place. We tried out a cable on the Pacific at great cost to Canada and the other contributors to the proposal, though ultimately, I believe, it proved successful. Canada owes it to herself, and the Mother Country owes it to herself, to have no more transactions with privately-owned cable companies, but immediately to build our own cables, or as soon after the war as possible. If we are in a position to-day to hold our own in this war and control the cables, it is not because of any prevision on the part of Canada or the Mother Country. Most of our cables are privately-owned, but they happen to land in the Mother Country, and very properly the Mother Country has taken possession of them. I think it is the case that the cables of the world are practically owned by a large corporation in the United States, probably the same corporation that controls the Bell Telephone. The great menace to the world to-day, especially in these times of war, is that the entire cable service is in the hands of private corporations. It has been repeatedly brought 'to the attention of the House that it would 
be in the interests of Canada and the cause we have at heart to bring .these utilities under public ownership. I pointed out many years ago that the greatest monopoly in the world at that -time was the Eastern Cables Company when it was controlled from England. It had great influence with the bankers' institutions and with the British Government, and in every other direction. There would always be two or three directors who were ministers of the Crown in the Mother Country. Up to to-day that company has absolutely succeeded in preventing the inauguration of an Empire-owned cable between the Mother Country and Canada. There are cables to-day between Canada and Newfoundland and the Mother Country (but they are owned by the great monopoly which is controlled from Boston ,and no effort is being made to break that monopoly. It is practically the strongest in the world to-day, stronger, perhaps, than the metal combine with headquarters in Germany.
There are two or three cable companies; are they all under one control?

They are all under one control. There is a telephone, a telegraph, and a cable monopoly in the United States, and they are all under one management, and that management is outside of the Empire although they do the Empire's business. We are continuing to trifle with this question. I wish I had the report of the Royal Commission here. Has the minister a copy of it?
'Mr. HAZEN:	Not here.

It was distributed in blue-book form to the members only the other day. In any event the commission reported in favour of an Imperial cable service. We all know that the merit of a publicly-owned cable service is that it gives a wide service at cheap reates; it does not exist to make profits, but the privately-owned cable has been used largely for profits and not for service.
I approve of what the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) did when he was Postmaster General to get a reduction in cable rates, but he did not proceed in the right way, and we are npt proceeding in the right way to-day. If we wish to serve the Empire we must get control of the cables. There is cheap telegraphy in parts of the world to-day because of State ownership, and if we wish to strengthen the Empire and

bind it together I know of no more effective way than a state-owned cable system, for the reason a cheap cable service is of great importance in the forming of public opinion. What is the ruling force in the world to-day, and what will be the Tuling force when this war is over? It is public opinion. And you can only get an immediate transfer of world-wide public opinion by a cheap cable service placed at the disposal of the press for the transmission of news and of opinion. But we have not got it yet. For some reason there is always some private company coming along to paralyze the effort for a national system of cables. What I said when this matter was first introduced in the House is confirmed by the report of the Royal Commission, which has reported in favour of a' world-wide system of state-owned cables. At present we are dealing with the Marconi Company. That may be a good company, but it has been on the boards a great number of years now, and it has spent a great deal of money, and you never know when they may fall into the hands of a bigger combine. There is no protection to the public' at all, except the splendid protection afforded by control of the landing stations.
What was done in the United States? There was a great wireless system' direct between Germany and the United States. Probably it was privately owned. Some sort of censorship was exercised over it by the American Government, but nobody knows to what extent that wireless system was used against us, and we never shall know until the war is over. But the day came when the American Government took hold of the landing station and the apparatus in the United States, and that has probably had a great influence on the war. But we are still continuing to deal with private companies; we aTe letting them make money, and every now and' then we get terms and concessions from them, but we are not getting what we ought to get. We talk about winning the war, and taking care of our interests and strengthening our world-wide influence, but we shall not make any headway until we avail ourselves of public ownership of the cables. Until we do that, we have not learned the lesson, and we shall not achieve any substantial results.
Again I urge upon the Government not to be a party in any sense to helping the private companies. Let us have public ownership, public control, and public construction of cables for the benefit of the Empire
and for the benefit of the 'business of this country. It does not cost much to build cables. There is at least one great cable-layer in the service of the cable companies, and probably more, and there are great plants which make a business of manufacturing cables. But they are all in private hands; they are all in collusion; they are all interlocked in one way or another. Perhaps some of the great newspapers have been in the combine. One cable for the relief of the world was started by newspaper influence, but it fell into the hands of the combine. That is the situation to-day.
In this war the great wireless service was in the control of the enemy, the office in the United States was in the control of the enemy, and wireless messages were being sent for the benefit of what proved to be the enemy, and we do not know yet what happened, because the American Government cannot expose what they discovered going on in that wireless service for the benefit of people who proved to be the enemies of the United States. I think that out of this situation, and out of the good understanding which has been reached be-* tween Great Britain and the United States, the time, has come-and this is the time- to have a publicly owned wireless service, and to take advantage of any and every different line of service, to get them into the hands of the State and the Empire. We must prevent an enemy, or a foreign country, controlling this service. The business itself can be best developed by public ownership and public direction, and by making it part of the great system of Imperial communications. That French word " communication " is a good word, in that sense which applies to all this great service, [DOT]and public communications of that kind ought absolutely to be in the control of the post office. I hope we shall soon have the land lines in this country. If there is to be such a service, and a distribution of public opinion daily by means of a cable service, it must be done, not only by state-owned cables, but by state-owned land lines, and right in our own country. We propose to improve the service for our papers by having a state-owned line in Canada, or by the Government leasing the wire from one of the private companies. Why not do away with this roundabout method and be up to-date and progressive, by having public ownership of these things? I have been in this House more than twenty years, and have been advocating public ownership for that length of time, but there is not much headway made yet, and there is no promise
With your leave, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say to my hon. friend-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has already spoken.
I know.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman may put a question but he is not permitted to speak again.

I wanted to make an explanation to my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean). My hon. friend seemed a little surprised at my attitude today having regard to the attitude I took when the Ocean Telegraph Bill was introduced a few years ago by Mr. Pelletier, then Postmaster General. My hon. friend states that then I advocated state ownership while to-day I do not offer any objection to a private company. I still stand for state ownership in this matter of cables and if it were not during the war I might perhaps urge upon the Government the necessity of having a state-owned cable under the Atlantic ocean. I wish to say further, that I suspect, as my hon. friend does, that there was some Ethiopian in the fence when that Bill was introduced by Mr. Pelletier. The Poulsen company has no standing in Europe to-day while the Marconi company is the only company that has made any progress in the matter of wireless telegraphy. If I support the Bill introduced by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, it is because I happen to know the personnel of this company. It is composed of men of substance and men of the highest financial and business standing. I think this country, as all civilized countries, owes a debt of gratitude to Marconi for the many lives he has saved on the wide ocean since he established his system for the equipment of steamships. Mr. Speaker, I am done, but I wish to remind my hon. friend that the rates for cables and wireless will now be controlled by the Railway Commission. The other day, when my hon. friend was away, I moved before the committee revising the Railway Act, that the rates on cables , and
wireless should be under the control of the Railway Commission, the motion was adopted and I hope the recommendation will be adopted by the House. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the indulgence.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time and the House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Blain in the Chair.
On section 1-Ocean Telegraph Act c. 52, 1913, repealed:

Four years have elapsed since we were promised a great service and this promise has not been fulfilled. What does the Government propose to do? Will the minister having charge of this Bill say whether he has read, or consulted with his colleagues in regard to, the report made by the Imperial Commission on the public ownership of cables?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This Bill is introduced after having been submitted to the consideration of my colleagues in Council. It is submitted with their approval, and, as it involves the return of money, it must have, and it has, the approval of His Excellency the Governor General. It simply seeks to repeal the Act of 1913 because the Poulsen company have failed to carry out the agreement they entered into. Their works-on which a very large sum of money has been expended-the company now being in liquidation, are to be taken over by the Marconi company which will make the necessary expenditure to make the plant and appliances efficient, and the work of transmitting cables from Canada to Bally'bunnion on the north-west coast of Ireland will be carried on. It is represented to me by the gentleman who represents the Canadian Marconi, and in whose bona tides I have every confidence, that the company will expend at least $100,000 on improvements to the plant at Newcastle in New Brunswick and another large sum on the improvements to be made at- Ballybunnipn, and they expect within a short time, with the improvements that they contemplate making, to be able to render very efficient service. The passage of this Act will in no way interfere with the consideration of the larger question referred to by my 5 p.m. hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) in regard to Government ownership of a cable line from Canada to Great Britain. As I understand it, the Post Office Department of Great Britain was not willing to consider in 1913, the establishment of another cable, in view

of the amount of money that was involved; but with this wireless system it was hoped that the country would get a system that would be of very great value without costing the country a single dollar. Up to the present time this has not cost the country a dollar and with the improvement to be instituted by the Canadian Marconi company they hope to be able to give an efficient wireless system across the sea. I agree with a great deal of what my hon. friend has said regarding this question, but it does not seem to me that the time when the efforts pf the country are being strained almost to the breaking point for, the carrying on of the war is the time to consider such a large expenditure as would be involved in the proposal suggested. This is one of the great questions that ought tp be considered. I myself am in sympathy with the idea of a cable line between Canada and the Mother Country that would foe owned and controlled entirely by the British and Canadian Governments.

I have listened with great interest to what the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has said. But, again, I point out to him, with reference to what he has said to the effect that for some reason the Imperial Government was not prepared some years ago tp go into this enterprise because of the expense, that it is the big monopoly that whispers this into the ear of the Imperial Government and every other Government. It urges the enormous expense of gping into this business in order to avoid a disturbance of its monopoly. We were told that four years agp when we struck out the monopoly and when we wanted to get cheaper rates. We have not got them but we have this report now from the Imperial Trade Commissipn which is printed in an English blue-book and the information in which is being circulated through the press. The cost is not so much and the cable will pay from the start if you put it where the paying traffic is. The paying traffic is between America and Europe. It would not lose a dollar. Even if we stepped in and cut the rates in two, the interest on every dollar of the investment would be paid twice over. While I accept the explanation of the minister, I am still looking for some initiative in the direction which we undertook four years ago but in regal'd to which we have not accomplished anything as yet.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext:
On motion of Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries), the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Blain in the Chair.
That it is expedient to amend the Meat and Canned Foods Act, chapter twenty-seven of the statutes of 1907, as amended by chapter thirty-eight of the statutes of 1910, and to provide, that all flsh and shellfish canneries shall be inspected, and all fish and shellfish packed in cans shall be subject to inspection during the whole course of preparation and packing, and marked- and labelled as prescribed ; that the canning of any particular fish or shellfish unfit for human food may be stopped at any time, and that all fish and shellfish used for canning shall be sound, wholesome and fit for human food, and unsound or unwholesome fish or shellfish may be seized on view by any inspector; that the size and contents of lobster cans and the designation of British Columbia salmon shall ibe as prescribed; that canneries not complying with the law may be closed; that no person shall offer or accept for export or shall export any fish or shellfish subject to inspection unless the requirements of the Act to -be based on this resolution and of the regulations regarding inspection and marking have been complied with, and proof is furnished as to inspection and marking; that all canned fish or shellfish imported into Canada shall be labelled as prescribed, unless imported to be exported again; and that any can of fish or shellfish not so labelled or marked before being offered for sale shall be forfeited and may be seized.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
About two years ago, the
administration of the Meat and Canned * Foods Act, so far as' concerns canned fish and shell-fish, was transferred from the Agricultural Department t-o the Department of Naval Affairs hy Order in Council. It was felt that the carrying out of the operations of the Act so far as concerned fish and shell-fieh would be better done under the administration of the department which has charge of the fisheries. The work has been carried out up to the present time by the fisheries inspectors throughout the country without additional salary. It has been found that in connection with their ordinary duties it is quite possible for them to inspect the different canneries, having regard to the provisions of the Meat and Canned Foods and Fish Act. But our experience during the past two years has shown that. the Act requires a number of amendments to make it adequate for the fish canning business1, and it ie for this purpose that I am asking the House to adopt this resolution and a Bill to be founded on it.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What is the meaning of the reference to the British Columbia salmon?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The statement that they
are to be as prescribed, means as pre-ecri'bedi in the Bill. That refers to the fact that in British Columbia there are a great many varieties of salmon, the cohoe, the humped back, the spring run and the dog salmon. We are going to change the name of the dog salmon and the humped back salmon. The names by which they are now known have actually had an adverse effect upon their market value. People think that fish with such names must be inferior. We are going to classify them in a different way. In another Bill, to amend the Fisheries Act, we intend to change the name of the dogfish. That fish is an excellent article of food when canned, yet no one will eat it dn our country, and if it were canned and placed on our markets no person would buy it. In the United States they are now canning the dogfish in very considerable quantities as an article for human food. They have changed its name by resolution to the greyfish-it is a fish of a greyish colour-and we propose in a Bill amending the Fisheries Act to change the name of dogfish to greyfish so that there shall be one name in universal use on this side of the Atlantic ocean, a name that will not convey an objectionable idea.
Mr. KY'TE:	Is not the minister perpetrating a fraud upon the public?
(Mr. HAZEN: I do not think so. A rose by any other name will smell as sweet, and I think the dogfish will smell much sweeter as a greyfish than as a dogfish.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Is it not a Shakesperian fraud? What's in a name?

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Is the minister going to ' authorize the canning of dogfish?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: There is no objection to it under the existing law. The objection is a practical one, that if you can it and ca'l it dogfish no one will buy it.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Is there any canning done now under the name of greyfish?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Very little I think. There have been' some experiments. One beneficial result of the canning of this fish will be to reduce its numbers. It is at present a very serious menace to all other varieties of fish, as it is very voracious, being in fact a small shark.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Why does the minister propose to specify the size of the lobster
cans? Is that done with respect to other fish?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I think that the sizes of
cans for other fish are prescribed now.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Have the lobster canners been consulted?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Yes. Before the amendments were finally decided upon, copies of a draft Bill were sent to those engaged in the industry and the amendments have been under consideration of the department and-of the Fisheries Advisory Board for nearly two years. Both the department and the board strongly recommend the adoption of these amendments and they have ibeen decided upon in the light of the criticisms received upon the original draft to which I have referred.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
To whom were they
sent?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I venture to say that all of those engaged in the industry in a large way received copies.
iMr. SINCLAIR:	Have the Fishermen's
Associations made any recommendations to the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The Fisheries Advisory
Board, of which a large number of fishermen are members, have very strongly reported in favour of the Bill.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I understand that the Fisheries Advisory Board is a departmental body.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
It is appointed by the
department and is composed of men who, serving without remuneration, meet two or three times a year and consult with the officers of the department with regard to practical fisheries questions.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Will this proposed legislation require the presence of an inspector in each canning factory?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It does not involve any additional expense. The work can be done by the' present officers of the department.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: How can that be, having regard to the terms of the resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I think that our officials have time enough to do it. I will give more information on that subject later.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
In my county we have four fishery inspectors and at this season of the year about 25 factories are in operation. Is it intended that those in-

spectors, within their own divisions, shall assume these duties, in addition to those which they already perform?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The language of the Bill is not that the factories shall be inspected, but that they shall be subject to inspection during the whole course of preparation and packing. It is open to any inspector at any time to go to one of these factories or canneries and see that the work is being properly done. The Bill does not require that he stay there and watch the whole operation.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: That is his duty now, under the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It is not the duty of our fishery inspectors now. When the Act was passed it had no reference to inspection under the Canned Poods Act, which was placed under the administration of the Department of Agriculture. Our inspectors were appointed for other purposes. The administration of that portion of the Act which has regard to the fishing trade having been placed under the administration of our department, it is necessary for us to pass an Act giving our inspectors additional power with regard to the inspection of these canneries.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: There are about 150 miles of sea coast in my constituency and along the harbours there are 25 or 30 packing places. Only two inspectors are available to cover that whole length of. coast, and if an inspector were to spend a day or so in each of the factories, about the best he could do would be to call about once a month. Even then he would be doing a great deal of travelling and be kept very busy. The inspection, therefore, will be very perfunctory indeed; inspection during the whole course of packing cannot be done by the present staff of officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: They have really done no inspection in the past along these lines.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The inspector calls at the lobster factories to see that the law is carried out; that the canning place is kept clean, and that seed lobsters are not packed. I do not think that the present staff of officers can do any more than that.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Were not certain regulations passed by the department some years ago fixing the standard with respect to the equipment and care of lobster factories, and were the inspectors not asked to carry out these regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I think there was something of that kind.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: This resolution provides that all fish and shell-fish canneries shall be inspected; I assume that that is being done now. While the fishery officers in Nova Scotia are, no doubt, efficient in the discharge of their duties, I scarcely think that they are sufficiently expert to carry out the duties imposed upon them by this resolution. The lobster factories extend over a large territory, and the fishery officers find it rather difficult to get over the ground within the fishing season. I can scarcely imagine that one fishery inspector would be able to carry out very effectively in his district the regulations provided by this resolution. While the employment of additional inspectors for this work is not contemplated by the minister, I assume that he has in mind the increasing of some of the salaries of the fishery officers who are to discharge the duties mentioned in the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I shall go more fully into the details when we are in Committee on the Bill. Before the Bill comes to its third reading I shall consider whether it is desirable that this matter be referred to the select standing Committee on Marine and Fisheries. The subject might receive fuller consideration in that way than it would 'be the Committee of the House.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Hon. J. D. Hazen thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 73, to amend the Meat and Canned Foods Act.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

On motion of Hon. J. D. Hazen (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) the House went into committee to^ consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Rainville in the Chair:
Besolved,-That it is expedient to amend the Fisheries Act, chapter eight of the statutes of 1914, and to provide that no one shall operate a fish cannery for commercial purposes without first obtaining an annual license therefor on payment of the prescribed fee; that the provision requiring that in British Columbia the site of any reduction works engaged in the manufacture of oil or other commercial products from sea-lions, sharks or dog-fish, is not to be within fifty miles of any other reduction works used for a similar purpose, shall be repealed; that fish guards in British Columbia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory, shall be provided where the minister

may deem necessary in the public interest; that no one shall leave any port or place in Canada to fish outside the territorial waters of Canada for fish the catching of which is at such time prohibited in the territorial waters of Canada opposite to or nearest the place where such person proposes to fish, and no one shall bring into Canada any fish caught outside the territorial waters of Canada when fishing therefor is prohibited inside the territorial waters of Canada opposite or nearest to the place where the same was caught, or shall bring into Canada any vessels, boats, nets, fishing gear, implements or appliances used in such fishing, but the rights granted to the citizens of any foreign nation by any treaty or convention shall not be thereby affected; that the name " dog-fish " shall be changed to "grayflsh," and that when the minister so requests, full and particular returns shall be furnished by every fish-curing or canning establishment or fresh fish business, fishing vessel, weir or trap owners.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The object of the resolution is to make certain amendments to the Fisheries Act. The first section of the Bill that I purpose introducing has reference to the licensing of fish canneries. It is to be provided by that, that:
No one shall operate a fish cannery for commercial purposes without first obtaining an annual' license therefor from the minister. Where no other fee is in this Act prescribed for a cannery license, the annual fee for each such license shall be one dollar.
At present the Fisheries Act requires salmon canneries and lobster canneries to be licensed; it does not require licenses from any other class of fish canneries. The canning of clams is now being carried on to a small extent, there being, I believe, about half a dozen such canneries in this country. There are a number of sardine canneries, and the canning of haddock, herring and other fish is being conducted in a small way, but gradually growing. The object of this requirement is to have all canneries properly enrolled so that the department can adequately follow their operations. The Meat and Canned Foods Act applies to them, and the fishery officers are required to see that its provisions are carried out. The fee is merely nominal, so that there will be no objection from that standpoint. This requirement was recommended by the Advisory Board, and its object is to place all canneries on the same basis as lobsters and salmon canneries, by requiring them to take out a license and putting them under the control of the department.
The second section refers to the question of fish guards, and that is a subject that applies to the provinces of British Columbia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory, where at the present time it is
absolutely obligatory under the Act for all irrigation ditches to be screened. In places where irrigation works are being carried on and irrigation ditches running into streams or into canals, it is necessary that there shall be a screen placed at the outlet* of the irrigation ditch for the purpose of preventing fish from the stream or canal from gbing into the ditch and thereby being destroyed. Several of these ditches are so located that' they are not dangerous to the fisheries, and as screens need to be under constant supervision to prevent their becoming clogged with debris, the existing requirements put the owners to much useless expense and trouble. The amendment leaves the requiring of such screens with the minister, as is the case regarding the fishways in dams throughout the country.
Is there any danger of that in the Yukon?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Yukon is mentioned as one of the places where there are irrigation works, but I must say that until I saw this memorandum, I was not aware that any such works \<rere being carried on there, and I would not think it was at all likely. As it is now, it is obligatory that these screens be placed in all those ditches, and it has been found that in a large number this serves no good purpose. Therefore, we want the matter to be left so that screens will be put in those ditches where necessary, and that owners of land and ditches where screens are not necessary, shall not be compelled to go to the expense of putting them in.
The object of the third section is to enable the department properly to control regulative fisheries which are partially conducted outside and partially inside territorial waters. Our Act and regulations cease to be effective at the outside limit of the territorial waters, but by preventing boats leaving the shore to fish outside at a time when they may not fish inside, or of [DOT] bringing to shore fish taken outside at a time when such is not permitted inside, the position can be controlled.
Will the minister state what kind of fish that refers to?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
During certain seasons of the year, there is a close season for lobsters; no one can fish for lobsters during that time within the territorial waters of Canada, that is to say, within three miles from the shore. But there is nothing to prevent any one from going outside the three mile limit and carrying on fishing operations, thereby greatly injuring the



fisheries at a season of the year when lobsters are in what is known as the soft state, that is, when their shells are not completely formed, or when they are breeding.
Would not those lobsters be liable to seizure when brought into a harbour?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is the situation. Up to the moment we have not actually found it impossible to prevent fishermen from fishing outside when they may not fish inside, but such is being talked of more and more, and it is desirable that we should have the necessary power to prevent it. Although we have prevented it there may be doubt that we have the legal power to do so; we want to make really lawful what we have actually been doing for the protection of the fisheries in that section.
Will the minister say whether, under the present law, he is not entitled to seize fish caught outside the three mile limit?
Men are constantly being fined for having lobsters in their possession out of season.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is very grave doubt as to our right to seize such fish. The next section refers to dogfish. Dogfish is now admitted to be a good fish, but its name is against its being commonly used. In the United States the name has been legally changed to "gray-fish," and it seems desirable that this name should be adopted in Canada as well.
The next section is to assure the obtaining of' correct statistical information. All the information contemplated is at present being procured by the fishery officers, but as it is not obligatory on those engaging in the industry to furnish it, sometimes it happens that it is delayed or that difficulty is experienced by the officers in procuring it. There is nothing new in the information asked for, the provision merely making it obligatory that such information shall be furnished so as to enable the officers to get it without trouble. So far as the lobster fishery is concerned, such information has been for years required by law, but it is not required by law with regard to other fisheries.
The last section is merely to harmonize the section with section 4 hereof,-by substituting the name "grayfish" for "dogfish."
It might be desirable also to have this Bill referred to the Committee on Fisheries, so that perhaps more careful consideration [Mr. Hazon,3
might be given to it than is usually accorded a Bill in Committee of the whole House.
Is there any scientific reason for this name? Is there not a fish called the grayfish?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is a grayling, which is a small sporting fish, and is caught, I believe, quite extensively in the streams and lakes of British Columbia. Then there is a fish found in New- Brunswick, in Loch Lomond, as to which scientific opinion is divided as to whether it is a grayling or originally a salmon, that got locked in those waters and has since deteriorated in size. This new name has been adopted in the United States.

How are you going to compel people to use this name?
Mr. HAZEN.- I think they will soon get the habit.
Do I understand that the regulation as to the quantity of fish caught is to be compulsory?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: Is any penalty provided for not filling in the return?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is a provision in the Fisheries Act providing penalties for violations of the law, and I think that would cover the case my hon. friend mentions.
I may say that these changes are recommended by the fishery offioers.
Has this information to be given under oath before a magistrate?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is no provision at
present requiring the information to be given under oath.
Resolution reported, read the first and second time, and concurred in.
