Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
Hon. J. D. .REID (Minister of Customs) moved the second reading of Bill No. 67, to amend the Customs Act.

May I .ask whether the Government of Manitoba have been advised of the intention to introduce this- measure, and whether there has been any correspondence with them in regard to it? Otherwise, it -seems to me, this Parliament should not be called upon to take away from the provincial government of Manitoba the legal right which it now possesses. The enactment of retroactive legislation of any kind is objectionable, and can only be justified in extreme cases for the purpose of removing an injustice of .some sort. I think that retroactive, legislation which expressly declares its intention to be the taking away of existing legal rights should be most carefully considered. The Crown in Tight of the province of Manitoba has -certain privileges and rights, and has had them ever since Confederation. Speaking the other night my hon. friend said that a certain practice had grown up and that the question of the legal status of the province in regard to payment of duties to this Government had not been raised. One can very readily understand that. In early Confederation days public ownership of public utilities was not thought of, and the imports of any one province for any particular purpose would be infinitesimal, and naturally the question of the payment of duties- would not be raised. But as the years went on the provincial governments assumed various powers, and their importations have necessarily increased. In Manitoba, for instance, they have a government telephone system, and the whole trend of legislation, particularly in the West, has been in the direction o-f governmental control; consequently there have been importations 1344
of goods which in the older days would not have been thought of. So much for the general principle.
My hon. friend also told us in the dbbate on the resolution that the Manitoba government and two other provincial governments had previously raised the quesiton, and that again recently the Manitoba government had expres-sly a-sserted that they were not called upon to -pay these duties, and that there was no right under the law to make them pay thfcm. This Bill expressly takes away from them their right of action.
Oh, no.

Then what is the
object of the Bill? I rose more particularly for the purpose of ascertaining whether this legislation was being passed behind the back of the province of Manitoba. I certainly think the Attorney General of the province should have been notified; the ordinary courtesies as between governments require that that should be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This Act is declaratory, and, so far as it i-s declaratory, it declares what the law was in the past, and I suppose, therefore, may have applied to it the word " retroactive." The hon. gentleman complains of this provision being made retroactive, and he explains, in his argument in support of his attack on the retroactivity of this measure, precisely why there should -be no objection to the retroactive provision. This measure is retroactive only -in so far as it enacts -that the Customs Act is to be read as applying to the Crown. It is not retroactive at all in any other respect.	,
That is a pretty important respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That happens to be the point which this province raised, or on which it contended it was not liable. The hon. gentleman says they did not do it in the past, because they had small importations, and it was not worth while. It is only as to the past that it will be retroactive. It is not retroactive for the growing commerce, which is coming in the future. The hon. gentleman claims there was not any object in raising the question in the past. It is only as to those cases in the past where the provinces themselves, as the hon. gentleman explained, did not think it worth while to raise any question, that this enactment will be retroactive. All that it will do, in so far as it is retroact-

ive, will be to prevent the province raising a question they never thought about raising for the purpose of recovering hack from the Dominion money which they paid voluntarily. They quite acquiesced in the right of the Government to collect this money. The real, substantial question which arises between the provinces and this Dominion is whether there is power in Parliament to impose customs duty on importations made by the Crown in the right of the province. Who is right or who is wrong in that question will not be affected in the slightest 'degree in this legislation; because, as I pointed out the other evening, we shall have no .more power to impose taxation on the Crown, if this be taxation, and we shall have no more power to collect customs duties from the Crown in the right of the province-if that power is vested in ns under the British North America Act- because we mention it here, than we had before. As regards the substantial question at issue between the provinces and the Dominion, this legislation will not alter the position one iota. If, before this legislation. Parliament had no power to impose duties on imports into the provinces, it will have no right now. . The purpose of this legislation, so far as it is to take effect in the future, is to place the question beyond doubt, that to the extent that Parliament has power, it is exercising that power to impose duties upon importations by the Crown. The retroactivity of the measure produces only this result: that the province will not be entitled to demand a refund upon a ground that it never dreamt of raising, and which it has not raised to the present day, but bases the argument upon the purely technical pretext that the Crown was not mentioned in the statute. The province will not be entitled to demand from the Government a refund of the customs duty, which, in the past, the province has paid, as the hon. gentleman says, because the duties were not worth talking about. I do not know whether that is correct or not. Whatever their reasons were, in the past they paid voluntarily, without raising any question.
Has Manitoba refused to pay the customs duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Manitoba proposes to bring in certain merchandise, and claims that it conies in free of duty. The contention of the province of Manitoba will not be affected in the slightest degree by the retroactivity of this legislation. I am

informed by the Minister ot Customs that that is what has taken place just now, and it will be covered by the Act when it becomes law. So that this bugbear of retroactivity amounts simply to this: we come now to provide-and in our opinion it is necessary-that our duties should attach.to the importations of the Crown, and especially mention the Crown, in order that, when we are dealing with this particular matter, the provinces will not be enabled to say to us, "Technically you had no right, because the Act did not mention the Crown, and we want our duties back."
Have any of the provinces imported any goods duty free in the past?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So far as I can ascertain, duties were paid upon whatever dutiable goods the provinces imported, and they raised no question until this particular point came up, save on one occasion, in 1909, and at that time the contention on the part of the Government making the claim was not accepted by the then Government of Canada, and, if I understand rightly, they submitted to the law. They have always paid duties'in the past. .

Does my hon. friend not think, in view of the apparent conflict that would exist between the federal and provincial authorities in this connection, that some time should elapse before the Bill is passed, and that there should be some official correspondence between the various provincial government so as to apprise them of the danger?

I do not think we should
[DOT]postpone the operation of the Act for that reason. The provincial governments, when they were importing goods, claimed that under section 125 of the British North America Act, they should not pay the customs duty. We replied, of course, taking issue with them as was done in 1909 and again in 1916. They then asked for a fiat. I am advised by the Justice Department that there should be a provision that goods imported by the Crown are dutiable, and it has been the practice for many years to treat them as dutiaible. The Dominion Government has been importing goods and duties have 'been collected for a number of years, but still the law' does not say the Crown shall pay duty, and the same system has been in force, in so far as the provincial governments are concerned since Confederation, and yet there has never been a provision in the Customs Act that the Crown

should pay duty. As I understand, the issue is now being raised. It made no difference, so far as the Dominion Government was concerned, if any question were raised, because it would be one department as against another, but now the provincial governments, which are the 'Crown also, raise the issue, and, as I understand it, the issue will be tried ont in the courts.
It is the duty of the Dominion Government to put itself in a proper position when the issue comes before the courts. Then, when we have on our statute book the provision that goods imported by the Crown for the Dominion or the provincial governments are liable to customs duty, the question will be tried out before the Privy. Council as to whether we have the right to collect customs duties on goods imported 'by the Crown in the right of the provincial government.
You want to bar action by the provincial governments?

No, they havg the right to take action without the consent of the Dominion Government. This does not prevent them going on with their action exactly the same as if the statute had not ibeen passed. But the Privy Council will decide whether we can legally collect t'he duties after having placed on the statute book a provision that provincial governments are liable.
Although you admit that you cannot collect now because the Crown was never mentioned in the Tariff Act.

I do not admit anything of the kind. I say that we can, but at the same time they have raised the issue that we cannot. To put ourselves in a proper position when the-issue is raised before the courts we ask that a provision be put on tjie statute book that the Crown is liable for duty.
And that it has always been liable?

As far as the retroactive part of it is concerned, if the Privy Council decides that the British North America Act entitles us to collect duties on goods imported by a provincial government for the reason that we have inserted in the Act a provision that they are liable, then the provincial government may come back with a claim from Confederation up to the present time, because at the time of Confederation we had not mentioned in the Act that the Crown should be liable for duty. The British North America Act. having been
interpreted by the Dominion and provincial governments in a certain way up to the present time, and no one ever having raised the question that is raised now, if the Privy Council decides that we have that right, it does not seem fair that the provincial government should then come along with an action simply because it was not inserted in the Customs Act at the time of Confederation that the Crown should be liable.

The question seems very simple. I remember a case that arose in the time of the late Government. The question was raised by one of the provincial governments as to whether they were liable for duty on goods imported by them. They claimed that they were exempt. We thought that in these modern days the Crown, like everybody else, should pay duty. The provincial government paid and the matter rested there. This Bill is to make it clear and certain that the Crown is liable, like every one else?
That is it.

Very good; I agree with the Bill altogether, but if you have collected moneys in the past illegally, or if you have exercised powers which you ought not to have exercised under the law, what reason is there why you should not refund the money? You cannot keep the money that you are not entitled to. The Government cannot give such a bad example to the community.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the second time, and the House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Rainville in the Chair.
On section 1-Duties payable on Crown's goods.

I would suggest that
my hon. friend allow the Bill to stand. The title of the Bill as introduced gives no indication of its purport; it is called simply a Bill to amend the Customs Act. If the minister -intituled it a Bill to take away the rights of those provinces who have paid customs duties oil goods imported for the Crown in respect of the provinces, that would have given some indication of its purport. But who would imagine that in a Bill to amend the Customs Act this retroactive provision would he inserted, intended to take away rights which may have accrued during the last fifty years, ever since Confederation

I do think my hon. friend would be well advised to allow the Bill to stand for a short time in order to give an opportunity for the provinces interested to jpe heard* I am told by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) that he has communicated with the Government of one of the provinces affected, but there has not been time to obtain a reply. It may be that no objection will be made, but it is a serious matter to pass retroactive legislation. The Prime Minister seemed to recognize the other niglpt the force of that objection and said he would think it over and see whether our views could be met. The difficulty about retroactive legislation is that while it may not do any particular injustice in the present case, perhaps ten years from now somebody may come to Parliament with some measure retroactive in its character, and when objection is made it may be said: why in the Parliament of 1917, with a careful member like the Minister of Customs, retroactive legislation was introduced; the Prime Minister approved of it, it must be all right, as he would not think of doing anything wrong. It has a bad effect, it is injurious and unwise legislation which should never be resorted to except where it is absolutely neccessary in the public interest.
Sir THOMA'S WHITE:	It is not bad
legislation in this case.

It is in this case. My hon. friend says it is necessary in the public interest to take away the rights of the provinces. I cannot agree. I would likp to agree with the Minister of Finance but I cannot in this case. Am I to understand that the Prime Minister has not given favourable consideration to the objections made? If it is intended to press the Bill through the committee to-night, I shall feel it my duty as one member to interpose any possible objection that can be raised.

I explained the situation just before six o'clock when the hon. member was not in. I have discussed the measure with the Prime Minister since it was up a short time ago and with the Justice Department again, and we feel that it is not doing an injustice to the provinces. Let me again explain the Bill as I understand it. This is an old question. In 1909 the Customs Department heard of this matter for the first time, when the deputy provincial secretary of the Nova Scotia Government addressed a letter to the Prime Minister in which he raised the question. He said:

I am directed by the Provincial Secretary to inform you that the customs authorities here have been claiming and collecting duties on goods belonging to and imported by the Government of Nova Scotia. It is submitted that the property of the Crown as respects the province is not subject to taxation, and the Provincial Secretary would be glad to have your views on the question.
The following reply was sent to the Provincial Secretary by the Commissioner of Customs:
I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the ISth instant respecting customs duties on goods belonging to and imported by the Government of Nova Sootia. In reply, I am to state that goods imported by or for the Provincial Government are subject to duty under the Customs tariff.
We heard nothing more about it until last year when the question was again raised" by the Quebec government and the same reply was sent to them. The matter rested there for a while, when the Manitoba government raised the question and we took the same stand, in each case having laid the matter before the Department of Justice. Now lately the Alberta government-
Have they been notified of this legislation?
Not of this legislation, no.
You propose to take away their rights without notice?

Therefore they have
been illegally collected on two grounds.

Not necessarily. We say not illegally. We interpret section 125 of the British North America Act as meaning that the provinces are not entitled to import goods free of duty. The reason we want this legislation is to have it in the Act that the Crown must pay duty. Then, when the case comes before the Privy Council, that is one point that must be decided, whether a provincial government is liable for duties under the Customs Act.
That is all right for the future.

Yes. As for the past, from
Confederation up to the present, that is the. interpretation which both the Dominion and the provincial governments have placed upon section 125. Nova Scotia did raise the question in 1909, but immediately dropped it.
Mr. PUGSLEY.:	Alberta and Manitoba
have raised it.

They are raising it now. If it is decided that we are within our rights in collecting duties upon goods imported by,the provincial governments, as we have done since Confederation, the provinces have no right to ask that they be reimbursed for the duties that we have collected in the past.

Their claim might be
supported on two grounds, one of which you wish to legislate from under their feet.
The Justice Department advised me strongly that this is the position we should be in if the matter goes to the courts.

We assume that the gentlemen who occupied the position of Minister of Justice in the past- were aware of that most ordinary principle of law that the Crown is not bound -unless it is expressly named. Parliament has never provided that the Crown as represented by the provinces should pay duty on goods imported by the provinces. Parliament, therefore, has recognized that under the Act of Confederation it is not right to compel the provinces to pay customs duties. The right of the provinces to reimbursement would rest on two grounds:	First, that Parliament had no authority under the British North America Act to impose (the tax; second, that Parliament during the fifty years since Confederation has not imposed
the tax. The question is about to toe raised in a court, and the minister is frightened. He thinks that, although the provinces may be wrong in their interpretation of the provisions of section 125 of the British North America Act, yet, because Parliament never provided that the Crown should pay taxes, the province^ may [DOT]be entitled to recover their money. He asks the Minister of Justice, therefore, how to get around this. The Minister of Justice says: a very easy way to do it is by passing retroactive legislation taking away the rights of the provinces and declaring that the position shall be as if fifty years ago Parliament had made the Crown in the right of the provinces liable to the payment of customs duties. The minister purposes doing this without setting forth in the title of his Bill anything indicating its design' and without giving the public the slightest intimation of what the proposed legislation is intended to accomplish. Nor does he notify the parties to the litigation of what is proposed.
There is no litigation.

My hon. friend says that some of the provinces applied for a fiat; does that not mean litigation? A person having a claim against the Crown presents a petition to the Minister of Justice asking for a fiat. If the Minister of Justice thinks the case should be dealt with in the Exchequer Court, he recommends to the Gov-erno/ General the granting of a fiat. The fiat is granted, and the proceedings aiie thereby commenced. If this were a matter as between private parties, Parliament would never intervene by passing legislation without giving both parties an opportunity of being heard. Yet the minister, because his party has a majority in this Parliament, proposes arbitrarily to take away the rights of the provinces by enacting this retroactive legislation, without the provinces having the slightest intimation of what is intended or the slightest opportunity of being heard. 'This proposed legislation is of a most objectionable character, and should not be passed. If my hon. friend's whole desire is to raise the question, let him enact this law for the future; then if the provinces import any goods they will have to rely solely upon the provisions of section 125 of the British North America Act. Any other course than this is absolutely unjustified, and I am sure would not have been recommended to Parliament by any Minister of Justice in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There never was a case which more clearly called for retroactive legislation, or more amply and completely justified such a course, than this. I should like to take my share of the indignation which the hon. member for St. John has poured upon the Minister of Customs. In justice to the Minister of Customs, I may say that he did not come to me and ask me for a way around this. I am entirely responsible for the suggestion of the legislation that has been condemned in such unmeasured terms-and I am not in the least ashamed. The provinces never raised this question at all; never suggested it; never had it present in their minds.
How could you tell?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If they did, they kept it in their minds and concealed it. They put forward only one contention: that they were not liable to pay duties under section 125. In the correspondence looking to a fiat or to some other method of legal proceeding, they never suggested this ground in the slightest degree. Since Confederation, Customs Acts have been passed applicable to all importations without exception. Importations by the Crown were not specifically mentioned, but, notwithstanding that fact, the Crown in the right of the Dominion clearly understood and admitted that the duties applied to themselves and to the Crown in the right of the provinces, and the provinces as clearly understood that, because they paid the duties without demur.

Is it not true that it is only within the last few years that the Crown in the right of the Dominion has begun to pay customs duties, and was it not a matter of expediency so as to show what were dutiable goods that came into the country? I venture to say that for forty years the Crown in the right of the Dominion never paid a cent of duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am told that about, ten years ago the Crown in the right of the Dominion began to pay customs duties. I referred to the Crown in the right of the Dominion having paid, but it is not from that that I deduce that the Crown in the right <jf the Dominion believed they had a right to impose the duties. I believe they so understood from the fact that they collected the duties. Of course, the Crown in the right of the Dominion paying the duties is a mere formality in any event; that is a matter of the Crown in the right of the Dominion taking money out of' its right hand

pocket and putting it into its left. As to the question between the Crown in the right of the Dominion and the Crown in the right of the provinces, there is just one Crown after all, and the distinction is one between the Dominion revenue and the provinces being subject to contribute to that revenue.

Is not the ground upon which the courts found that where the Crown is not expressly named in an Act of Parliament, the Crown is not bound, based upon the idea that Parliament did not intend to include the Crown?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is what it is based upon.
It was not the intention of Parliament to include the Crown.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I assented when the hon.. member said he assumed, but actions speak much louder than mere assumptions, and the hon. gentleman says that the Ministers of Justice knew that that statement ought to have been in the Act, and that because they did not put it in we must take it for granted that they did, not intend to do so. .Marvellous to relate, we must take that for granted of all of those successive Ministers of Justice with the assent of all the successive ministers, their colleagues, including the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), who sat in a Government the Prime Minister of which authorized the writing of a letter, in 1909, to say that those duties were legally collectable and refused to recognize the claim of the provinces. It is a serious imputation of bad faith upon the gentlemen who conducted themselves in that way for the hon. member to say: Oh, they knew all the time, and they fully intended all the time that there should be no liability. I say that their actions talk; I do not make such an imputation upon them.
I was speaking about Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's distinctions are exceedingly fine. The hon. gentlemen is speaking of Parliament, but when he was speaking of what Parliament intended, he found it necessary, in order to demonstrate what Parliament intended, to fall back upon the argument that the successive Ministers of Justice knew that that statement ought to be in express terms; and that they did not put it in the Act and put the matter to Parliament in that way, therefore, says the hon. gentleman, Parliament deliberately intended not to in-

elude the Crown. Let me point out to him that the actions of all those successive Ministers of Justice shows what is the real fact, that it was the purest and merest oversight. Oversights have occurred in other cases, and I have not the slightest doubt that this was a pure oversight, and the action of all the successive Governments of the Dominion, including all the successive Ministers of Justice, show that it was an oversight ; that they were not doing what the hon. gentleman said; that they were not, with the knowledge that omission left the Crown out, asking Parliament to pass Acts that were not to apply to the Crown. What happened was that there was this oversight, but the whole line of action shows that the intention was that those duties should be applied; and it is as fair to assume that Parliament knew that those duties were being applied, as it is to assume an intention based upon a purely technical rule of law, and, I think, will bring us to the truth. The matter was one of public notoriety; everybody knew it and everybody acquiesced in it. We must assume that successive attorneys general of the provinces knew that very simple rule, and still the provinces all acquiesced in it, and everybody recognized that this was a proper thing to ask for on the part of the Dominion Government and a proper thing to pay on the part of the provinces. And, now the hon. gentleman rises in indignation

The minister is aware in making his argument, which will practically serve as an estoppel, that it was not until 1895 or around that date that it was settled as a matter of law that the Crown existed is connection with the provincial Government. It was not until the maritime bank case was decided Dy the Privy Council and it was held that the Crown was present in provincial governments and that the Lieutenant Governors were not merely officers of the provincial governments. My hon. friend's argument, therefore, could not apply until after that was settled.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is about twenty-two years ago. And in the first place, might I suggest that the judgment of the Privy Council was known. Does the hon. gentleman not think there were some lawyers and some attorneys general and some Ministers of Justice in this country who knew what the law was before the Privy Council came to a decision. The Privy Council did not make law; it decided what the law was, and I myself had the pleasure of
knowing a large number of very distinguished lawyers in this country who had not the slightest doubt that the Crown was a part of the legislatures of the provinces.
It would have been remarkable, seeing that was the law, that we should at that time have produced no lawyers who knew it.
The Supreme Court of Canada decided the other way namely, that a lieutenant Governor was merely the representative of the Governor General.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Supreme Court of Canada made a mistake. We. are being condemned because it is to be assumed that every Minister of Justice knew the law and had his mind on it and therefore did a particular thing. That is the argument of the hon. member for St. John. The hon. member for Pictou wants us to be condemned because we must admit that before 1895 all the attorneys general of the different provinces did not know the law or were mistaken about the law. I cannot see any great force in that argument, and I think ' it is a remarkable fact that if their acts rested upon a mistake in 1895, we have never, down to the present day, or to this moment, had a breath of suggestion from the provinces that they were not liable because the Crown was not mentioned in the statute.
They have not suggested that, and it is on their behalf that it is suggested now for the first time in this Parliament. This propossed legislation results from the fact that it was thought wise when the provinces raised one particular contention, resting their claim: entirely upon that, and when because they raised that there was the possibility of our being brought into court, to guard against their ever raising this purely technical ground of which they had never thought and have not raised up to the present day. I entirely fail to see why there is ground for indignation because we propose to "close the door against people coming now with belated claims to recover money which the Crown in the right of the Dominion collected in the past in perfect good faith, and which the Crown in the right of the province paid perfectly willingly. That is all we are seeking to do by the retroactivity of this legislation. To give sanction to what everybody understood to be the law, we are going to declare that the law was what everybody understood it to' he.

And what my hon.
friend does not think it was.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think there wae an
oversight. I want to give the hon. gentleman the full .benefit of what he said and repeated a great many times. The provinces may have a right, upon a pure abstract technicality, to recover back money that was collected from them in good faith by the succeeding governments of this Dominion, and which they .paid perfectly willingly and .quite voluntarily. Technically, they may have the right to do that, because what they understood to be the intention of the law, what this- Parliament and the Government of Canada understood to be the intention of the law, was by oversight inadequately expressed. The indignation- is all because these provinces are having the door closed to their raising a claim to recover money that was collected quite honestly and paid without question, always leaving out the question of the power of this Parliament to impose those duties, which does not come into this legislation at all. What we propose to do is simply to give the sanction ^ of this Parliament to everybody's understanding of the law during that long period of years, and not to leave the door open to the questioning of the application of that law so understood merely because there may be a technical ground upon which all these things that were done in the past in. perfectly good faith might be disturbed. That, to my mind, is the ideal case for declaratory or retroactive legislation. This does not prejudice any right of the province in the future. It does not prejudice any rightrof any province to recover anything that it has paid upon the one ground which no. province has ever invoked as entitling it to recover-on the ground that under the British North America Act there is no power in this Parliament to impose the tax.

My hon. friend seems to forget that the people of these provinces are not estopped by any failure there may possibly have been on the part of their government to assert a right. My hon. friend forgets the principle that the Crown is never estopped.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I never talked about estoppel at all. It was the hon. member for Pictou who interpreted my words as referring to estoppel. I never claimed anything as resting on an estoppel at all.

I am sure the minister was perfectly well aware that the Crown was never estopped by delay or by laches. [Mr. Pugsley.t
What its rights ever were, unless they have been released in some way, those rights still exist. The minister says that the governments of these provinces legally and properly paid what they ought to have paid, and that the claim that they might recover is purely technical. I fail to understand upon what .ground the minister bases that contention. Either the provinces have the right to this money, or they have not. If Parliament has never imposed a tax upon them, surely their right to recover is not technical. Bear in. mind that' it is not the governments of these provinces who are to be debarred from, their rights by this legislation; it is the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is the people of this Dominion whose rights we want to protect.	-

It is the people of the provinces who make up this Dominion, and to my mind it is scandalous for the Dominion Government to take advantage of its paramount power of legislation to take away the rights of the provinces. I am surprised that for such a comparatively small amount as is involved, a few thousand dollars, this Parliament will be called upon to exercise its paramount power of legislation and take away a right which may exist on behalf of the people of the provinces. That is not technical; it is substantial, and I care not whether any of these Governments has failed to put its claim on the two grounds. If there are two grounds, the fact that a Government has failed to put its claim on both grounds ought not to prejudice the people of the province. The men who are acting to-day are acting on behalf of the people of those four provinces, Alberta, Manitoba, Quebec and Nova Scotia. Now what have the people of those four provinces to do with the omission on the part of men who happened to be in the Government ten years ago, to put their claim on two grounds? If they have a claim on two grounds, what right has this Parliament to take away the claim, absolutely valid and absolutely legal, which, they may have upon one ground, and say they must rest their case entirely upon the other ground? This Parliament has no right to do that, just because it is allpowerful, and that is the only ground upon which the Minister of Justice can put it. He can say, "We are all-powerful. Under the British North American Act we have the power to take away rights which exist to-day in the provinces; we can alter our

Customs Act; we can pass a law to-day and make it run back for fifty years and say that that which has not been the law for the past fifty years shall by the Act of this Parliament to-night be deemed to have been the law." Yet the minister says that is purely technical. Although the people of these provinces may have the right to get their money back, because, forsooth, some of those who represented them in the past did not put their claim on two grounds, the minister says, "We will deprive them of one ground, which we fear is a perfectly legal and valid ground, and see that they do not recover on that ground at all events," simply because they did not put forward their claim as they might have done.	..
Notwithstanding all my hon. friend ha3 said, I am unable to see why this legislation should be passed. If this Parliament wants to legislate that the provinces shall in future pay duties on goods which they import, let it legislate for the future. Then as to any duties which may be exacted in the future, the provinces will have to rest their claim upon one ground only, namely, upon the provisions of section 125 of the British North America Act. But if they have two grounds which they have a right to avail themselves of in the courts of the land, surely this Parliament ought not to take away their rights. It is proposed to do this without notifying the provinces-doing it behind their backs. This Parliament has no right to do that Retroactive legislation is most objectionable under all circumstances, and can only be justified by the gravest necessity; and surely the mere fact that the Government thinks that there may be a few thousand dollars which, as the result of the litigation may go to the people of these four provinces, is no ground for the Government resorting to an exercise of its power and asking Parliament to pass legislation extending back fifty years.

I am surprised -at the
lack of information on the part of the Government in regard to the concrete cases which brought about this legislation. I quite agree with my hon. friend beside me that this Parliament has full power and authority to state who shall pay the duties, and who shall not pay the duties. I believe that the Crown, in the right of the Dominion Government, could stipulate by whom the duties should be paid, but it seems to me that, when the minister introduces legislation, retroactive in its nature,
the least that we might expect from the Government is that some regard should be shown to the provinces. If there is one thing which the Federal Parliament should avoid it is litigation with the provinces. It seems to me the provincial and Dominion Governments should have most happy relations [DOT] and should avoid conflicts. We all know in the past from what small causes arose the very stringent fights which took place between the Ontario legislature and the Dominion Government. We know how long these cases lasted, that they went to the Privy. Council; in fact, the result of those cases was the creation of a party of provincial rights in Ontario. In such a small matter, when everybody conceives that the Government can state who shall pay the duties, it seems to me we. should avoid giving the legislation any retroactive effect. I do not refer to the correspondence of 1909, but can the minister tell me what were the concrete facts which brought about this legislation? Has, there been notice given by the minister to the various provincial governments that this legislation would be brought down this session?
I have not given the provincial governments any notice that it was my intention to bring this legislation before Parliament during the present session.
What are the concrete facts which cause this legislation?

The reason that I am putting the measure through this session is this, as I stated: In 1909 the master came first before the Government of the day, and the right hon. leader of the Opposition, then Prime Minister, took issue. The provincial government did not raise any further question, and the matter dropped. It was then brought up last year by one of the four governments, and I sent the same reply, word for word, that was sent by my predecessor in 1909. The matter again dropped, and .then another provincial government brought the matter up, and the Manitoba Government stated that they wished to take issue with the Dominion Government; that is, they wanted a fiat. Of course, they could proceed in the Exchequer Court, and it would not make any difference whether they got a fiat from this Government or not.
Was there any entry made in the. customs in Winnipeg in regard to this matter?
Yes, they made an entry.
They imported what?
They imported a gas producer -that is the way the item is described- in August, 1916. The duties were $404.80, and when it came in they took issue on paying the duties on that machine.

Has the minister any
record of the grounds on which the Manitoba Government based their objection? Was it simply that they were not bound to ,pay the duty, ,or did they base it on section 125?

On section 125 of the British North America Act.
, Mr. PUGSLEY: Have you their letter to that effect?

Yes. The letter reads as fol-. lews:
Winnipeg-, Aug. 23rd, 1916. The Honourable, the Minister of Customs, Ottawa, Canada.
Re Gas Producer Plant at Souris, Man. Sir,-
On the 10th inst. I wrote the Commissioner of Customs, Ottawa, in regard to a charge of $404.80 duty on a gas producer plant which was purchased by the Provincial Government of Manitoba in England and was entered through Souris in Manitoba.
Payment of the $404.80 was made under protest as the contention of the Provincial Government of Manitoba is that no duty is chargeable on said gas producer plant.
The province of Manitoba now wishes to make a formal demand for the repayment of said $40-4.80 from the Dominion Government on the ground that section 125 of the British North America Act prevents the Dominion Government from charging such a duty on such a gas producer plant owned by the Provincial Government.
In case of your refusal to pay back this $404.80 I take it yours department will be glad to have the matter passed on judicially. The province of Manitoba will at once institute proceedings in the Exchequer Court of Canada to recover the said sum paid for duty.
I shall be glad if you will indicate your decision in the matter as early as possible.
1 have the honour to be, -Sir,
Your obedient servant,
John Alien,
Deputy Attorney General.

Suppose they had two grounds of objection, and only put forward one, surely you would not take away the other ground? The substantial point is that they say they are not liable for the duty. Suppose they have a dozen reasons, and only put forward one, they are entitled when they go to court, to raise the dozen grounds.

The hon. gentleman asked
why I was putting the legislation through this session. The case referred to arose in

August last, and I submitted the matter again to the Department of Justice, and consulted my colleagues in council. 'The provincial government stated in their letter that they would like to have it tried judicially. I do not want to have it tried judicially, because I take it for granted the matter is settled; but if they do proceed, the Department of Justice says that, in order to have the question tried as to whether we can collect customs duties from the provincial government this provision should be in the Act.

Is not the real issue whether, under the then existing law, this Government had the right to exact duties from the provincial government? Whether they base their claim on one reason or a dozen reasons there are only arguments that apply.
We claim that we have had the right to collect these duties since Confederation.*'
You admit by this statute that you think you had not the right.
No, we do not; we claim that we have alwaj^s had the right to collect duties under section 125.
Well, then rest on the law as it is.

No, I will not rest on the law as it is. I am not a lawyer myself, but as a layman I think I am entitled to my own opinion and it is that in order to have the matter decided in the Privy Council it is just as well, and it will probably assist our case, to have on the statute book the claim that the Crown is liable to duties.
Mr. P.UGSLEY: Of course, that will assist you because you have taken away one ground of action which the provinces had against you.

Well that is something the Department of Justice arid members of the council think should be done. Why, make it retroactive?-the hon.. gentleman may ask. We are only declaring in the statute tnat the law, as interpreted by the Dominion and Provincial governments since Confederation, has been that the Crown was liable to pay duties.
This would bar them from their action.

No; if the Privy Council decide that the provincial governments are not obliged to pay customs duties, no customs duties will be collected, our declara-

lory act will have no effect and they will have a claim for any duties which have been paid since Confederation. On the other hand, if the Privy Council declare that we have a right to collect duties on goods imported by the provincial governments, I do not think that it would be fair that they should have a claim simply because this declaration was not put in the Act at Confederation.
Then the Bill assumes that you have collected duty illegally?

I 'do not interpret it in that way because it has been admitted by the Dominion and provincial governments that that is not a proper interpretation but that it is the result of an accident or a technicality.
No, it is not a technicality.
It was a technicality in that it was not put in at that time to make it plainer. However, we are all acting in the interests of the whole people, both the Dominion and the provincial.
You are not acting very much in the interest of the provincial Governments.

I do not agree with the hon. gentleman. There is' only one ground of difference in the committee, as far as I can see. There is no objection to this Bill going through and having effect
9 p.m. from the present time onward but the whole objection appears to be that it should not be made to apply to all time since Confederation.
It should not interfere with existing rights.

I claim that if the Privy
Council decide that we cannot collect duties from now on, after it has been recognized since Confederation that we were entitled to these duties, it would be better to have this clause put in.

It is rather difficult to follow hon. gentlemen- in dealing with this matter. I fail to see where the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) or the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid), have met the point made by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley). What is the position of the Government on this question as declared by the Minister of Justice? He says: "We have had the right to collect customs duties on goods. imported by the provincial governments from Confederation
.down to date because they have never objected to it until within the last few years." The Minister of Justice, in dealing with the point that I called his attention to, made no answer when I suggested to him that it was only within a period of twenty years-not fifty years-that it has been settled as a matter of law that the Crown is present in the provincial legislatures.
Previous to 1895, do I understand the hon. gentleman to say, the provincial governments did not consider that they were a part of the Crown?

It w*as so urged by those who were advocates of the belief that the Confederation Act had created in this Federal Parliament a certain central authority and that the, governors of the provinces were simply Dominion officials and as such were not authorized to exercise the prerogative of the Crown. It was decided by the Supreme Court of Canada in the case of Lenoir and Ritchie, known as the King's Counsel case, that the provincial governments had no right , to appoint these counsel as the King was not present in the provincial legislatures. So that when my hon. friend says that the provincial governments did not raise this question during the whole period of fifty years, I say it was not until twenty years ago that it was decided absolutely that the Crown did exist in connection with the provincial legislatures. Only then could they be aware that the Crown in right of the province was exempt from the provisions of the law if in the law it was not specially named. My hon-. friend says that if the provinces did not raise this question before they ought not to be permitted to raise it now.
No, they can raise it now.

My hon. friend says that if they do raise it now they ought to be met by an Act of Parliament which declares that for the last fifty years the Crown has contravened the Customs Tariff Act and therefore its right is taken- away. Does the minister propose to pass this retroactive legislation to say that because a particular province did not sit down and prepare what might be called a petition of right, or a statement o-f claim in which their legal position is maintained and set out, they cannot raise the ground and it does not meet the point? If litigation is taken they could raise this ground, together with the general ground that it falls within section 125 of the British North America Act and that there-

fore the duty could not be collected or imposed. They might raise both of these grounds or any other ground that these litigants would have the right to raise. This country has no right to pass retroactive legislation to anticipate the remedy which Manitoba, 6r any other province might seek to have in court, and to declare to have been the law in the last fifty years that which was not the law. It is useless for my hon. friend to say it was a technicality and an oversight. Either it was that the Crown in right of the Dominion for fifteen years deliberately taxed the Crown in right of the province, or it was not. I was surprised to hear the Minister of Justice argue upon that point. The Minister of Justice knows very well that the principle which, declares that statutes do not apply to the Crown unless it is especially named, is not a technical principle at all. Very important and far-reaching rights rest upon that principle. No Parliament from 1867 until to-day has undertaken to declare that the Crown's name should be .mentioned in a tariff Act. If the province of Manitoba wants to import goods, tractors or engines in connection with their agricultural or experimental farms or apparatus for the use of their telephone system or any other public work, they have a right at this moment, as I understand the law, to import them without- having to pay customs duties. My hon. friend by this legislation is coming in to say that, although they had imported such machinery last August, they must pay duty now. That is ex post facto legislation, it is retroactive, and it takes away the rights of the province. For that reason I object to it. I submit further that this question having been raised, as the province of Manitoba is seriously raising it, the minister should have advised the proper authorities of that province of the fa.ct that this legislation was being introduced so that we could discuss, it intelligently and be in a better position to decide whether what appears to be obnoxious and improper retroactive legislation should be placed upon the statute book. I think the request of the hon. member for St. John (Mt. Pugsley), that the Bill should stand over until the views of the governments of Manitoba and Alberta can be ascertained, is well founded.

I submit to you, Sir,
and to the Minister of Justice, that the rights of the provinces and the Tights of those who are governed under the British North America Act should be settled by

the courts, if necessary by the Privy Council, through the proper interpretation of the British North America Act, and not by any Act that we might pass in interpretation of it. The rights of the provinces and the rights of the Governors of the provinces are fixed and established by the British North America Act, and it is by the interpretation of that Act that any doubt that may have arisen as to the rights of a province should be determined. We should not attempt to give that Act any twist or turn, or to make it anything different from what it was when it -left the hands of the Imperial Parliament. We should submit it to the courts as it has been submitted in every other case where it has had to be interpreted, in its purity. We should not pass an Act interpreting it and then'send the two to England to be passed upon. I submit that it is no argument to say that because a local Government or any other body has been making a mistake for forty or fifty years they are thereby forced to continue making that mistake, or to continue to pay' out moneys which they should never have paid. I remember a very in; teresfing case in Nova Scotia relating to a lockup at Spring Hill, which was tried before Sir Robert Weatherbee, one of the most distinguished lawyers in this country. The people of Spring Hill had been using a lockup for twenty-five years a building which really never was a lockup. Sir Robert in his facetious way said: It is argued before me that the people of Spring Hill niade a mistake twenty-five years ago; that they fiave persisted in that mistake for twenty-five years, and that therefore it has become legal. Of course he swept the thing aside as being nonsensical and not worthy of legal argument. As Sir Robert Weatherbee then said so, I think we should hold now. The Minister of Justice should advise that it is no argument to say that because the provincial governments took it for granted that any demands made upon them by the Federal Government were right and, without looking into the law, paid the demands made upon them, and then when they came to look into it and found that they were making a mistake during all this time, the Dominion Government could set up what is practically a plea of estoppel.
Returning to the Act itself, the words " tax " and " taxation " are used everywhere where reference is made to the collection of duties. The word " tax " is used in section 91 of the 'British North America Act. In giving the powers of this Parliament, it says:

The raising of money by any mode or system of taxation.
The word "taxation'' is usually under-/ stood in the provinces and elsewhere as the ordinary taxes. When we talk about taxation, we very seldom think of customs duties'. But in the British North America Act, duties are spoken of as a tax; they call it "tax," they do not call it "customs . duties." Then we haVe the power under - section 91 of the British North America Act' to get money by any mode or system of taxation. If that was the only thing in the Act, no doubt we would have power to tax any property that was held in the right of the Crown. But section 125 says:
That no land or property-
The word "property" there includes everything that could be stolen.
No land or property belonging to Canada or any province shall be liable to taxation.
The word "taxation" is used there. In section 125, the word "taxation" has the same meaning exactly as in subsection 3 of section 91; and if we are going back to the intention of Parliament, we must take it for granted that the intention of the Imperial Parliament in the beginning, in 1867 when they passed this Act, was that any property held by' the Crown in right of a province or any property held by the Crown in right of the Dominion, was not subject to any tax whatsoever, either by customs or otherwise. Therefore, if any tax has ever been collected by this Government from the provincial governments upon any property that they may have been importing that ordinarily would be subject to taxation, they were collecting if in good faith, I presume, but by a mistaken conception of the law. I wish to point out to the Minister of Finance, as a constitutional lawyer and a man who has to do particularly with finances, that to me, who do not profess to be a great constitutional lawyer, it is very clear that under the Act the Government has no authority to levy any tax upon any property belonging to the Crown, in the right of either the province or in the Dominion; that subsection 3 of section 91 simply used the word "taxation":
The right of raising of money by any mode or system of taxation.
Therefore, taxation covers everything, any way in which we may get money. If that is all that was in the Act, we could, I suppose, tax anything. Section 125 says:
No land or property belonging to Canada or any province shall be liable to taxation.
The word " property " applies to anything that has tangible existence or value; anything that can be used or appropriated. Instead of giving a long list, therefore, of things exempted, the farmers of the Act used the comprehensive word " property." The gas producing machine or engine that was imported into Manitoba certainly is property and, being owned by the province in the right of the Crown, is exempt from taxation, including customs duties. The Government, then, had no right to collect duty upon it. The proper thing to do when we discover the true meaning of a law is to forget the past and to proceed with a proper administration of that law.

The hon. gentleman contends that the provincial governments have the right under the law to import goods with out paying duty. When the right hon. leader of the Opposition was Prime Minister, he and his followers took the ground that the provincial governments should pay duty on these articles. The only way to settle the matter once for all is to have the Privy Council interpret the Act.
Mr.McKENZIE: But it should be settled upon a proper interpretation of the original Act, not upon an Act now introduced.

This does not change the
Act at all..

Then what is the good of it? Are we playing with legislation? Have we so much tiftie that we can pass legislation that has no purpose or object? If we have the right to collect duties upon property entering Canada for the provinces, we have that right by virtue of the power conferred upon us toy the British North America Act. Let us have the matter interpreted by the courts, if there is any doubt about it, but do not make it more difficult by passing this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This Bill does not touch the British North America Act or its interpretation.
Inferentially it does.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Not inferentially,
directly or indirectly. The great object of the Bill is to make it quiite sure that the only question upon which the case will go to the courts and ultimately to the Privy Council shall be the interpretation of the British North America Act. It would be a childishly absurd contention that this Parliament, by any legislation of its own, could in any degree affect the powers conferred upon it by the British North America Act.
Will the minister tell the committee briefly what the Bill is for?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is for the purpose of declaring that the present Customs Act does, and that the Acts passed since Confederation did, apply to the Crown.
Then you are asking Parliament to make a false declaration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member for St. John does say such crushing things. He has told the member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) that we are doing a frightfully wicked thing. But has he not made it clear to the member for North Cape Breton that we are not touching the British North America Act; that our wickedness is all directed to the Canada Customs Act?

I never said that
stupidity was wicked.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You did say that the member for St. John said that the proposed legislation was wicked.

The hon. member for St. John has made the matter so clear from the standpoint of a constitutional lawyer that it is almost unnecessary for me to speak about it. The Minister of Justice - says that it is necessary to pass the Bill now under consideration in order to arrive at a proper interpretation of the British North America Act and to assert that we were right during the last fifty years in collecting these duties. *

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not at all. This Bill simply seeks to ma.ke the Customs Act read as though these words were in it: " This Act shall apply to the Crown." It goes no further than the Customs Act of Canada; it seeks simply to have the Act read as including words to the effect that it shall apply to the Crown. That is what everybody thought it meant; we want to make the law square wiith what everybody did and understood respecting it. I repeat that the 'Bill does not in any way affect the British North America Act or its interpretation. We shall have to determine what power this Parliament had under the British North America Act; this Bill says nothing about that. What the Bill .seeks to make clear is that Parliament exercised whatever power it did have.

I perhaps understand
the situation a little better, but it does not change the viewpoint at all. The Customs Act must find its constitutional foundation and right in the British North America Act, and if the Customs Act has gone any fur-

ther than it should go under the basic principles of our constitution, to that extent it is ultra vires and of no effect. We must take for granted that the able constitutional lawyers who were in this Parliament at. the time of Confederation and at the time that the Customs Act was drafted and put through this House were fully cognizant of their powers and authorities under the British North America Act, and that the Customs Act was passed in conformity with those powers. We have, therefore, no business now, by this new legislation, to import into the Customs Act anything but what was in it at that time, and we have no business to put any interpretation upon the 'Customs Act. The Minister of Justice says that this Act does not give an interpretation of the British North America Act, and I agree with him in that, but it does give an * interpretation as to what may be regarded as the. outcome or product of the British North America Act, and if either in the one case or in the other we are going beyond our rights to legislate, we have no right to do so, and the question reverts to the same point: what are the rights of the provinces under the British North America Act? The Customs Act does not alter the situation at all unless that Act comes with. in the purview of powers intended to be conferred uppn this Parliament. That is exactly where I stand, and I submit that this legislation should not be introduced at all until we get a decision of the Privy Council on the point. We have an illustration of this in the Bill that was introduced in this House this afternoon by the Minister of Finance. There was a dispute about the constitutionality of the Insurance Act, and as I understand it, the minister did not bring any legislation before Parliament to patch up the dispute; he waited until an interpretation was given to the matter by the Privy Council, and he then introduced legislation to implement so far as he could what was decided by the Privy Council. The same line of action should be followed in this case; if we are mistaken about an interpretation, we should apply to the courts and get the proper interpretation and after this is received, if it is necessary to change the legislation for the proper and practical carrying out of the Act, then let us get further legislation, but let us not go guessing about the matter now. In fairness and equity, it seems to me there should be no taxes upon the provinces. Take the simplest proposition where we have common jurisdiction and authority. Take agriculture, in which there is a jurisdiction that

is held in common by the provinces and by the Dominion. If the Dominion Government introduce into this, country a herd of cattle or stock for breeding purposes, they do not pay any customs duty, or they simply pay it from one pocket into' the other, so that they really have the advantage of paying no duty. The Department of Agriculture of a province may be doing exactly the same thing, but under the interpretation which is sought to be .put upon the law, they have to pay duty. From the beginning the intention of the Imperial Parliament was that goods -coming into the country in the right of the Crown should not pay duty, and it was a mistake right along to be collecting that duty from the governments of the different provinces. Perhaps they can recover that duty. I do not know whether the same principle that would apply to the individual would apply to the Crown. If an. individual pays any money by mistake of law, he can never get it back, and I presume the Crown would have the right to raise that point, although perhaps .it would 'be a technical objection and would not be worthy of the Crown when it is the Crown on the one side and the Crown on the other. I am not saying a word as to whether these moneys should be paid back or not. I am glad to have an opportunity of expressing my views with regard to the real interpretation of those points of the British North America Act and of the right of the provinces and the Dominion under them.

The Minister of Justice made a statement a moment ago which, I think, calls for some remarks. He says that everybody since Confederation has thought that the Customs Act applies to the Crown as represented by the provinces. I wish to deny that most emphatically. The only evidence he has given us of that is that in the statement of protest presented by one or two of the provinces they mention section 125 as exempting them from taxation. Surely that does not . prove that the people of the different provinces from which duties have been illegally exacted have assented to the view which the Minister of Justice now puts forward. Take the case of New Brunswick. My hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Copp) has called my attention to the fact that only a few months ago that province imported a large quantity of road machinery, and I have no doubt upon that they illegally paid duty. They have not made a claim on any particular ground to get that money back, and I presume the officials paid it because their attention was not called either to the omission of the Crown from the Customs Act or to section 125 of the British North America Act. This Government has illegally imposed a tax against the people of the province of New Brunswick in respect of a good many thousand dollars worth of goods which they have imported for the purpose of public improvement. I presume it will also be found that in respect to fertilizers, which the government of New Brunswick has been importing, this government has exacted customs duties illegally. It is said that the province no doubt has the right to recover that money as conditions are to-day. The province might rest its claim upon two grounds: first, that the Customs Act does not apply and has not professed to apply to the Crown, and secondly, that under section 125 of the British North America Act, this Parliament has no right to impose duties upon the provinces respecting goods im' ported by them. Have the people of New Brunswick ever waived their rights? Are they estopped? The Minister of Justice says everybody has thought that the law was as this government is now attempting to make it, but the people of New Brunswick have neveT expressed an opinion upon this point, either through their government or otherwise, and they can to-morrow put in a claim to recover these duties. Does this government say to them:	Although
you have two grounds on which to base your claim, we are going to legislate one of those grounds away from you? The minister says: Oh, the people of New Brunswick have always thought that the Customs Act -applied to the Crown. There is no evidence whatever of a waiver of whatever legal rights they have to-day to recover that money, and, as a representative of that province, I protest in the strongest manner possible against their rights being taken away by this legislation. The only ground upon which this government can take their rights away is that Parliament has the paramount right to do this injustice to the people of that province, if it chooses to do so.
I wish to prove what I said a moment ago, namely, that, the legislation is false upon its face, and this Government is asking Parliament to declare and place upon record what is known to be absolutely contrary to the truth. These are the words of the Bill.
The rates and duties of customs imposed by this Act or the Customs Tariff or any other

2! 34

law relating to the Customs, as well as the rates and duties of customs heretofore imposed by any Customs Act or Customs Tariff or any law relating to the Customs enacted and in force at any time since the first of July, one thousand eight hundred and sixty-seven, shall he binding,-
That is all right for the future.
-and are declared and shall be deemed to have been always binding-
That is a false statement. They have not been binding for thirty years.
-and are declared and shall be deemed to have been always binding upon and payable by His Majesty, in respect of any goods which may be hereafter or have been heretofore imported by or for His Majesty, whether in the right of His Majesty's Government of Canada or His Majesty's Government of any province of Canada.
I say that is a declarataion which this Parliament ought not to be called upon ter make. It is declaring that this Customs Act has been binding on the Crown in the right of the province. But the Minister of Customs knows perfectly well that it has not been binding; he knows that this Bill has been introduced because the Justice Department has told him that by reason of the Crown not being mentioned he has no legal right and never had a legal right to collect these duties. The Minister of Justice, as one of the best lawyers in the country, knows that this Customs Act has never been binding upon the Crown in the right of the province. Without suggesting there has been any doubt on the part of the minister himself or the deputy minister on the subject, and knowing perfectly well that these duties have been illegally exacted from the provinces, he is asking this Parliament to-night to take away the legal rights of the people of those provinces, and prevent them from having an opportunity of making a claim which they would raise upon both grounds. He is endeavouring to prejudice the people of the province making a claim against the Government by reason of the legal exaction of these duties.

Will not the minister permit this legislation to stay in committee until we hear from the Manitoba government on this question? As they have raised the issue I think the House ought to have the advantage of hearing their views,, and the province should be given an opportunity of presenting them before Parliament comes to a conclusion on the matter.

I cannot see any object in allowing the legislation to stand. My duty

is, of course, to look after the interests of the Dominion so far as my department is concerned. The government feel that this legislation should he passed in the interests of the Dominion. We cannot hope to ga'n anything by communicating with the provincial government. They will simply say, as they did in their letter that they ought not to pay the duties. We are anxious to get our legislation through as soon as possible, and as an opportunity has been given for every hon. gentleman to express his views, I see no object in allowing *the legislation to stand.

On account of its retroactive character this is not an ordinary measure. Whenever a Bill is introduced, whether by a private member or by the government interfering with vested rights or retroactive in its character, the House should be seized of all the merits of the case before it comes to a conclusion. It is upon that ground, a very reasonable and just ground, I think, that I ask that the measure be not pressed now. If the minister has confidence in his legislation, he can have no objection to waiting to hear from the provincial government on this matter.

I cannot see what is to be gained by holding this over, as we have all. the information before us that we can possibly get. It is simply a question of law, and if the provincial government wish to proceed with the case, they can of course go to the Piivy Council.
After you have taken away their rights.
I do not think we are taking them away, nor does the Department of Justice.

What is the Bill for
them?

The Government have considered this Bill carefully, and are satisfied that it does not interfere with the British North America Act. An opportunity has been given to hon. gentlemen to express their views, and I can see no reason why we should not advance the Bill.

I should just like to call the minister's attention to what the Supreme Court always does in a matter of this kind. If any question comes up affecting the rights of any province, they always insist on notice being given to the province, but here we are legislating behind the backs of the provinces. Remember, it- is

not individuals that the provincial governments represent, but all the people of all the provinces, and the people of the provinces will feel aggrieved that this legislation is passed behind their backs, with no opportunity being given to them for expressing their views.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have every respect
for the arguments that have been made, but I think I ought to say frankly just how it strikes me. The contention that there is any wrong or injustice being done to the province in this matter, it seems to me, is so clearly and manifestly futile that I should be ashamed to delay the legislation to hear them argue that there was an injustice. In the second place, I am satisfied that there is no argument that they could put before us, and nobody whom they could get to put that argument before us with greater skill than has been done here this evening. For these reasons I quite understand why the Minister of Customs does not feel disposed to consent to delay this legislation.

I think that the suggestion of my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) that this legislation should stand over until the provincial government is heard from is a reasonable and proper one. I do not propose to make any argument on the legal aspects of this case, because that has already been done so ably by my hon. friend from Pictou and my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley). It seems to me that there must have been a feeling in the minds of the hon. gentlemen opposite that the provinces have some claims. There may be some question about it, but it must appeal to them that the provinces have some claim in regard to this matter, and they are apparently taking the position: "What we have we'll hold"; we have this amount of money, small though it be, but a principle is involved; we have collected this amount of money for years from the different provinces in duties on goods imported, and, to make sure, we will pass an Act and hold what we have. That does not seem to me to be a reasonable proposition. I am not prepared to say which of the hon. gentlemen who have argued the legal matter is right, and it is more or less of an invasion, in my opinion, of provincial rights, and, therefore, it should not be decided hurriedly, in an ex-parte manner, by this Parliament. And they say: Although the provinces may have some rights, we will remove the foundation of all the claims that they have made. I understand that some
of the provinces have already made claims on the Government, that they have paid duties they should not have paid, and that they should be reimbursed this payment made by mistake. Four provinces, I believe, have already made claims in regard to the return of duties paid by them. I know full well that the province of New Brunswick last winter entered into a large contract with a firm in the United States for road machinery. Since that time the Government was defeated, and the succeeding Government continued the contract, and I think part of the machinery has been delivered, and the present Government will stand in the shoes of the late Government. Irrespective of the question as to which is right and which is wrong in regard to the legal aspect of the case, it seems to me it is an infringement of and interference with provincial rights, and, that being so, I think the provinces should be consulted and given an opportunity to state their case before the committee in a different manner, presenting their views to us.

What is the meaning of the last five lines of the section? It seems to 'be an anomalous proposition. My hon. friend declares that he proposes to institute a tax upon the provincial governments of Canada, and to declare it was the intention of Parliament that they should always be taxed. The last four lines read as follows:-
Nothing herein contained is intended to impose or to declare the imposition of any tax upon, or to make or to declare liable to taxation, any property belonging to His Majesty either in the right of Canada or of a province.
The imposition of this tariff on property brought into Canada by any provincial government is an imposition of a tax. Why have these anomalies, taxing at one end of the section, and declaring that they are not taxed at the other end?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In no part of the section do we impose a tax on the province or the Crown. We declare the Crown to be subject to the legislation; we do not declare any right on the property of the Crown. We propose to collect the duty from the Crown when the Crown makes an importation, and we collect it without regard to the ownership of the property. Perhaps hon. gentlemen have not fully realized that customs duties are imposed upon the man who imports, and he will have to pay them if he imports another man's property, just as much as if he imports his own property, and it is true, with regard to the individual, that there is a lien or right imposed upon

the property itself to secure the payment of the tax or duty. In so far as the right upon the property may possibly be interpreted to be a tax on the property, we have no intention of imposing any obligation on any property which belongs to the Crown, but all that we want to do is to make applicable to the Crown, as to every other person, the obligation to pay a duty when goods are brought into this country, no matter to whom they belong.
Is the duty not a tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
Is this not intended to
be a parliamentary interpretation of section 125 of the British North America Act or to assist in the final interpretation of that section?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Most assuredly it is
not intended to he. If it were intended to be, I would say it was one of the most awful failures I ever heard of.

What is the meaning
of it?	\

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The intention is' to
