make it perfectly clear that we 'do not in- * tend to create any obligation upon the property of the Crown. I might answer it better by saying that it means exactly and precisely what it says, and the hon. gentleman who is asking the question, who understands the English language perfectly, knows the meaning of it.

I have heard judges,
when they could not understand the language of a provision, state that it meant exactly what it said.
Mr.-GERMAN:	If the province of Ontario should import a thousand tons of steel for some public purpose, that thousand tons would be the property of the Crown as represented by the Government of the province of Ontario'. The British North America Act says that the property of the

Crown shall not be subject to a tax. Does my hon. friend propose now to impose a duty, which is a tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We do not propose to
.impose any duty, tax, or anything else on that thousand pounds of steel. We propose to say that whoever imported that steel shall pay a duty of so much, and the amount of that duty will be determined on the value of the importation.

What is the meaning
of section 2, which says:
If any imported goods seized in any building within one hundred yards from the frontier between Canada and any foreign country are forfeited according to law, such building shall also be seized and forfeited, and shall be forthwith taken down and removed.

There are buildings close
along the frontier, which parties use for storing goods which are brought in there in violation of the law, and there are some buildings partly on one side of the line and partly on the other. The United States Government has on its statutes a section which reads as follows:
If any store, warehouse or other building shall be upon or near the boundary line between the United States and any foreign country, and there is reason to believe that dutiable merchandise is deposited or has been placed therein or carried through or into the same without payment of duties, and in violation of law, and the collector, deputy collector, naval officer, or surveyor of customs, shall make oath before any magistrate competent to administer the same, that 'he has reason to believe, and does believe, that such offence has been committed, such officer shall have the right to search such building and the premises belonging thereto; and if any such merchandise shall be found therein, the same, together with such building, shall be seized, forfeited and disposed of, according to law, and the building shall be forthwith taken down or removed.
Our officers tell me that there are parties who use buildings in that way and that they rush goods over to the otheT side when the officers are coming or when they have information that they are smuggling. We are putting this clause in and it is similar to the clause in the Act on the other side of the line in the expectation that it will make it more workable between the two countries.
Bill reported.

Bill No. 66 to amend the Judges' Act- Mr. Doherty-read the second time and the House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Rainville in the Chair.

On section 1-appointment of puisne judge:
What is the salary of the judge now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no change in the salary. This is to add one to the number of'judges in Saskatchewan as provided for by the provincial legislature.
On section 2-appointment of county court judge:

Has the minister ever thought of making some provision, of course, in conjunction with the provinces, to have the county court judge in districts where there is very little litigation going on transferred to districts where their services might be required instead of appointing new judges? We all know that litigation has fallen off in the last few years in many localities. I am told it is so in Ontario and I know it is so in my own province. In some districts the judges have a good deal to do while there are other districts where they are comparatively idle, and instead of appointing additional judges and putting the country to a great deal of
expense, they might be distributed and in this way the work could be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This matter was adverted to by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) on the resolution introducing the present Bill. I explained then that some two or three years ago I had taken the matter up with the then Attorney General of Ontario and had represented to him the desirability of acting on the lines suggested by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley). At the time there appeared to be a disposition to listen favourably to what was suggested, but it has not resulted in any action. I did say, in response to the suggestion of my hon. friend from South Renfrew, that I would again take the matter up to see if something could be done on that line. As far as there is any addition here to the judiciary of Ontario, it is of a judge in Timiskaming which is a new and growing district.
